title: What a form asks you to hold in your head
description: Every field that references an earlier answer without showing it, every code you have to retype from memory, is a withdrawal from a working-memory budget that's already spent for a lot of your users before they open the page.

learningObjectives.text: Identify where a form requires the user to retain information across steps without redisplaying it
Apply WCAG 3.3.7 Redundant Entry to a real multi-step flow
Explain why blocking paste on a verification-code field increases memory load rather than reducing errors

contentSections.title: Redundant entry: making someone re-type what they already told you

contentSections.body: A landlord reference-check form collects full legal name and date of birth on step 1 of 5. On step 4, a field reads 'Confirm the name and date of birth you entered earlier' — two blank text inputs, nothing pre-filled, no way back to step 1 without losing the three steps of progress in between.

contentSections.scenario: A checkout collects a shipping address on step 2. On step 4 (billing), the form shows blank address fields with no checkbox, no pre-fill, and no link back to step 2.
contentSections.question: Does this meet WCAG 3.3.7 Redundant Entry?

options.label: Yes — the user already typed the address once, so it's already 'provided'
No — nothing on this screen auto-populates it or offers to reuse it
It depends on whether the user's browser happens to autofill it

feedback.yes: Typing it once doesn't satisfy the criterion — 3.3.7 is about what the interface does with information it already has, not what the user has already supplied somewhere upstream.
feedback.no: Right. WCAG 3.3.7 (added in 2.2, Level A) requires information previously entered in a process to be either auto-populated or available for the user to select, unless re-entry is essential or the earlier value was invalid. Blank fields with no mechanism to reuse the shipping address fail this outright.
feedback.browser: Browser autofill is a nice-to-have, not a compliance mechanism — it can be off, blocked by the browser, confused by custom-styled inputs, or simply never primed with the value. The criterion is about what the page itself offers, because the page is the only thing every user actually has.

contentSections.concept: **Redundant entry is a working-memory tax the interface charges on purpose.** A 'Same as shipping' checkbox that copies the value — checked or not — satisfies 3.3.7 because it *offers* reuse; leaving the field blank with nothing to select does not, even if the user technically 'could' remember and retype it. The criterion doesn't ask whether recall is possible. It asks whether the interface made the person do it.

contentSections.body: This matters more than 'mild annoyance' framing usually gives it credit for. Working memory under real-world load — pain, medication, interruption, a toddler in the next room — holds reliably somewhere around three or four items, not the '7±2' figure that gets quoted from research that's since been substantially revised downward. A form that asks someone to retain a date of birth *and* a reference number *and* which of two similar screens they're currently on already exceeds that budget before anything goes wrong. Every redundant field is a fresh withdrawal against a balance that was never large to begin with.

The fix is rarely difficult, which is part of why finding it in an audit matters: store the value in state once it's entered, then pre-fill or offer it wherever it's needed again, with an easy way to change it if it's wrong. The exception 3.3.7 carves out on purpose is re-entry that's *essential* — a password confirmation field genuinely needs a fresh, independent keystroke to catch typos, and a payment CVV should never be stored or pre-filled for security reasons. Naming which of those two situations you're in — genuinely essential re-entry, or just nobody built the reuse — is the actual judgement call in a finding, not just spotting the blank field.
If a form asks a second time for information it already has, that's not friction — it's a working-memory tax the interface didn't need to charge, and WCAG 3.3.7 says so directly.

contentSections.title: Verification codes: the field built to be impossible to paste into

contentSections.body: A two-factor login sends a 6-digit code by SMS. The code input is six separate single-character boxes, wired with `onpaste="return false"` — built, according to the commit message, to 'stop copy-paste typos.' Now every user has to alt-tab to the messaging app, hold six digits in memory, switch back, and type them one at a time before a countdown expires.

contentSections.scenario: The code field above blocks paste entirely. Support tickets about 'wrong code' errors go up after the change, not down.
contentSections.question: What's the actual mechanism behind more errors, not fewer?

options.label: Blocking paste doesn't cause this — six-digit codes are just hard to read from a phone screen
Blocking paste forces manual retention and retyping across an app switch — exactly the condition most likely to produce a transposed digit
Paste was never going to work reliably on mobile anyway

feedback.unrelated: The scenario is specifically a before/after change tied to the paste block — the mechanism is directly implicated, not a coincidence.
feedback.retype: Right. The failure mode paste-blocking claims to prevent — pasting the wrong thing, stray whitespace — is rare and minor. The failure mode it *guarantees* is everyone without perfect working memory retyping a number they just read on a different screen, under time pressure in many implementations. That's the condition transposition errors actually come from.
feedback.mobile: Mobile paste from a messages app into a web form works fine in every modern browser when it isn't deliberately blocked — this isn't a platform limitation, it's a decision in the code.

contentSections.mechanism: **A one-time code is exactly the case WCAG 3.3.7 allows re-entry for — which makes preserving the one thing that reduces its cost more important, not less.** Since re-typing the code is unavoidable, the interface's whole job is minimising how much has to be held in working memory while doing it: `autocomplete="one-time-code"` lets iOS and Android surface the code above the keyboard automatically, and allowing paste lets anyone who copies it manually skip retyping altogether. Blocking paste removes the one mitigation available for a field that was already going to be the hardest one on the page.

contentSections.body: The honest caveat: a handful of older banking and government systems still block paste on password and code fields as an explicit, deliberate security control, on the theory that it prevents credential-stuffing scripts from filling fields programmatically. That's a real trade-off some organisations choose to make — but it's a security decision with a cognitive-accessibility cost attached, not a free improvement, and it should be named as a trade-off in a finding rather than dismissed as an oversight if it turns out to be intentional.
A one-time code is the one field where re-entry is genuinely unavoidable — which is exactly why blocking the one shortcut that reduces its memory cost is the worst possible place to do it.

title: Consistency, predictability and the interface that moves
description: A control that shifts position right as someone commits to clicking it, or that changes its name three screens later, forces a re-read WCAG's context-change rules don't fully reach — and naming that gap honestly is part of the finding.

learningObjectives.text: Distinguish a genuine WCAG 3.2.1/3.2.2 context-change failure from a layout-shift problem the criteria don't cover
Apply WCAG 3.2.4 Consistent Identification to a component reused with different labels

contentSections.title: Buttons that move while you're aiming for them

contentSections.body: A settings form has a 'Save' button fixed at the bottom. The instant any value changes, a banner reading 'You have unsaved changes' slides in directly above it — pushing Save down 40 pixels right as the user, already moving the pointer toward where it used to be, commits to the click.

contentSections.scenario: Two interfaces. Interface A: a dropdown that, the moment a new option is selected, immediately submits the form and navigates to a different page with no warning. Interface B: a banner that slides in above a Save button, shifting it downward, triggered by typing in a field.
contentSections.question: Which of these is the kind of thing WCAG 3.2.1 (On Focus) / 3.2.2 (On Input) actually covers?

options.label: Both — any unexpected interface change on interaction is in scope
Interface A only — 3.2.1/3.2.2 cover context changes like navigation or focus shifts triggered without warning, not layout reflow
Interface B only — moving a button is more disruptive than navigating away

feedback.both: 3.2.2 is specifically about *context* changes — a new window, a page navigating, focus moving somewhere unexpected — triggered by changing a value with no warning. A layout reflow that doesn't move focus or navigate anywhere is a real problem but isn't what this criterion measures.
feedback.a-only: Right. Interface A auto-submits and navigates on a mere selection change with no warning — a textbook 3.2.2 failure. Interface B is a genuine, disabling problem for a lot of real users, and WCAG's Predictable principle simply doesn't have a criterion that reaches it, because nothing about focus or navigation context actually changed.
feedback.b-only: It's plausible B feels worse in the moment, but WCAG's context-change criteria are written around navigation and focus, not visual position — B sits outside their letter even where it's arguably worse in practice.

contentSections.concept: **This is one of the clearest cases in the whole phase of a barrier WCAG covers thinly.** A button shifting under a moving pointer, right as someone with motor slowing, tremor, or simple fatigue-driven imprecision commits to a click, causes real mis-clicks and real frustration — and there is no dedicated success criterion that names it, because 3.2.1/3.2.2 are scoped to *context* changes, not layout reflow. An audit that only checks named criteria will miss this every time; a good audit names it anyway, as a finding without a clean citation rather than one stretched to fit 3.2.2.

contentSections.body: The fix costs almost nothing once it's named: reserve the banner's height in the layout even when it's empty, so nothing else moves when it appears — a fixed-height container with `visibility: hidden` until needed, rather than one that only exists in the DOM once triggered. Alternatively, place transient banners somewhere that structurally can't overlap a primary action (above the whole form, not directly above one button) so their appearance never displaces a target someone is already moving toward.

3.2.1 and 3.2.2 cover context changes — navigation, focus jumps — not layout reflow. A control that shifts under a moving pointer is a real barrier with no clean citation, and it belongs in an audit anyway.

contentSections.title: Same action, different name, on every screen

contentSections.body: A profile-editing screen's primary button reads 'Save changes.' Two screens later, in the billing section, the functionally identical action — write these field values, keep the user on the same screen, show a confirmation toast — is labelled 'Update.' A third screen, notification preferences, calls it 'Apply.'

contentSections.question: Does WCAG 3.2.4 Consistent Identification require every screen to use the exact same word for the same action, or something looser?
contentSections.answer: Something looser — it requires the same functionality to be *identified* consistently (the same label, icon, or role used every time it appears), not one single word mandated site-wide. 'Save changes' used consistently everywhere satisfies it. The failure isn't 'more than one possible word exists' — it's the same action being labelled three different ways across a product with no pattern to it.
contentSections.hint: Think about what 'consistent' actually requires versus what it would take to lock down site-wide terminology forever — those are different asks.

contentSections.body: **WCAG 3.2.4 Consistent Identification (AA)** requires that components with the same functionality within a set of pages be identified consistently — the same label, the same icon, wherever the same thing happens. This isn't about branding polish. It's about whether a user can act on a pattern they've already learned instead of re-reading and re-verifying every single screen, which is expensive for anyone relying on procedural memory rather than re-parsing text each time — exactly the group most likely to be worn down by three different words for one action.

Predictability means the same action looks, is labelled, and lives in the same place every time — so a user can act on habit instead of re-reading, which matters far more when re-reading and re-verifying costs real energy.

title: Instructions that arrive after the mistake
description: A placeholder that vanishes the moment someone starts typing, a password rule that only appears after a rejected submission, an error banner miles from the field it's about — all three make the same trade: instructions the moment they'd help, versus instructions after they've already cost a wasted attempt.

learningObjectives.text: Diagnose placeholder-as-instructions as a WCAG 3.3.2 failure pattern
Apply WCAG 3.3.1 and 3.3.3 to locate and phrase an error correctly

contentSections.title: The instructions that vanish the moment you need them

contentSections.body: A password field's only guidance is placeholder text inside the input itself: 'Min 8 characters, 1 number, 1 symbol.' The moment someone starts typing, the placeholder is replaced by what they've typed — the requirement disappears at exactly the point they'd want to check it against what they're entering.

contentSections.scenario: A user typing a password can no longer see the format requirement once they've typed a single character, and submits a password that fails validation.
contentSections.question: What's the actual mechanism causing the failed submission?

options.label: The user simply didn't read the requirement before starting to type
Placeholder text is replaced by the user's own input, so the instruction is only visible in the one moment it isn't yet needed
The password field's contrast is too low to read the placeholder

feedback.userfault: This blames a design decision on the user. The requirement was genuinely visible for a moment and then genuinely gone — the design, not the reading, is what failed here.
feedback.mechanism: Right. A placeholder is designed to disappear on input by definition — that's what a placeholder is for (a hint for an *empty* field). Using it as the only home for a requirement guarantees the requirement is gone precisely when someone needs to verify their input against it.
feedback.contrast: Contrast could be a separate, real finding on its own — placeholder text is frequently too pale to meet 1.4.3 — but it isn't the mechanism behind a requirement vanishing entirely once the field has content, which happens regardless of contrast.

contentSections.mechanism: **WCAG 3.3.2 Labels or Instructions (A)** requires labels or instructions when content requires user input — and a placeholder used as the *only* source of that instruction fails it in a way that's easy to miss in a quick visual scan, because the field looks perfectly labelled the instant before anyone actually uses it. The fix isn't removing the placeholder; it's adding a persistent instruction — visible text below or beside the field, in the DOM the whole time — that survives the field having content, with the placeholder left as a genuinely optional example on top of it.

contentSections.body: The same failure shows up in a worse form when the requirement doesn't exist anywhere on the page at all until *after* a failed submission — the format rule only appears attached to a red error message, following a wasted attempt. For someone re-attempting this form with reduced capacity, that's not a minor delay: it's a full extra round trip of typing, submitting, reading an error, and holding the corrected requirement in mind while retyping — a repeat of the exact cognitive load from the previous lesson, caused this time by timing rather than absence.
A placeholder is built to disappear the moment it's needed. If it's the only place an instruction lives, the instruction is gone at exactly the point someone would check it.

contentSections.title: Errors that appear at the top of a page you've scrolled past

contentSections.body: A long registration form is submitted from the bottom of the page. An error summary — '3 errors found' — appears at the very top. The user's viewport is still scrolled to the submit button. Nothing moves focus, nothing marks which fields, nothing scrolls the page. The three errors exist; finding them is a separate task the interface hasn't started yet.

contentSections.question: Put these in the order a form should actually surface validation errors on submit.
steps: Move keyboard focus to an error summary (or the first invalid field) as soon as validation runs
List every error with a link or anchor that jumps to its specific field
Mark each invalid field visually with more than colour alone — an icon and text, since colour-only fails for anyone who can't reliably distinguish it
Keep the specific instruction next to the field itself, not only in the top-of-page summary
Preserve every valid field's entered value — don't clear the form because one field failed
contentSections.explanation: Each step targets a different way 'the error technically exists somewhere' fails to be an error someone can actually act on. Moving focus is what stops the error from being invisible to anyone not looking exactly at the top of the page. Per-field anchors and per-field messages are what stop 'find the error' from being a second, unassisted task layered on top of 'fix the error.' Colour-only marking fails independently of all of this — someone who can see the field is red but can't distinguish red from the surrounding UI still needs the icon and the words. And clearing valid fields punishes the one mistake with a second, larger one.

contentSections.body: This connects directly to **WCAG 3.3.1 Error Identification (A)** — the item in error must be identified and the error described in text — and **3.3.3 Error Suggestion (AA)** — where a fix is known, it must be suggested. 'This field is invalid' technically identifies an error and fails the spirit of both criteria in the same sentence: it says *that* something is wrong without saying *what* or *where*, which is exactly the gap that turns a fixable mistake into a second undirected search.
An error message a user has to hunt for is a second task hidden inside the first one — find the mistake before you're even allowed to try fixing it.

title: Error recovery without starting over
description: One wrong postal code shouldn't cost twelve correct fields, and one expired session shouldn't cost forty minutes of typed answers about someone's own medical history — the difference between those outcomes is almost always a small, specific engineering decision.

learningObjectives.text: Distinguish deliberate, justified data-clearing from accidental total data loss on a single field error
Apply WCAG 2.2.1 Timing Adjustable to a session-timeout pattern

contentSections.title: One wrong field, twelve fields lost

contentSections.body: A 12-field application form is submitted with one mistake: the postal code is in the wrong format. The response clears every field on the page, resets the security-check image, and starts the form over from empty — the postal code and the other eleven correct answers are gone equally.

contentSections.scenario: Two forms both clear a field on submission failure. Form A clears the CVV security code field after a declined card payment. Form B clears all 12 fields, including name and address, after a single postal-code format error.
contentSections.question: Which of these is a defensible clearing, and which is a defect?

options.label: Both are defensible — clearing on any failed submission is standard security practice
Form A is defensible (a payment security field genuinely shouldn't be retained); Form B is a defect with no equivalent justification
Both are defects — nothing should ever be cleared on a failed submission

feedback.both-ok: 'Security practice' genuinely justifies not retaining a CVV — but there's no equivalent security or privacy reason to also erase a correctly-typed name and address because a postal code's format was wrong.
feedback.a-ok-b-bad: Right. Not retaining a sensitive value like a CVV after a failed payment attempt is a legitimate, narrow security decision. Clearing every other field along with it — fields with no sensitivity concern at all — is simply a state-management shortcut, not a deliberate choice, and it's the one worth flagging.
feedback.both-bad: This overcorrects — there are real, narrow cases (payment security fields specifically) where not retaining a value is the right call, and a blanket 'never clear anything' recommendation would miss that distinction.

contentSections.concept: **The question in every case is whether the interface is protecting something sensitive, or just resetting a form object because it was easier to build that way.** Retaining a payment security code across a failed attempt is itself a minor security anti-pattern most payment processors specifically advise against. Retaining a correctly-typed name because a *different* field failed validation has no such justification — it's simply that clearing the whole form on any error was the path of least implementation effort, and the twelve correct answers pay for it.

contentSections.body: The fix, in most frameworks, is a matter of scope: validate and clear per field, not the whole form object on any single failure. State that's held independently per field survives a sibling field's error by construction — the postal-code field resets or highlights itself, the other eleven simply never get touched. This is usually less code than the version that clears everything, not more, because it stops treating the form as one all-or-nothing unit.

Clearing a sensitive value on failure can be a real, deliberate choice. Clearing everything else along with it is usually just an implementation shortcut, and it's the twelve correct answers that pay for it.

contentSections.title: The session that expires while you're still filling it in

contentSections.body: A benefits application has a fixed 15-minute session timeout with no autosave. A user spends 40 minutes on the medical-history section, thinking through how to phrase an answer, checking a letter from a specialist for an exact date. The session silently expires. Submitting logs an authentication error. Every answer is gone.

contentSections.question: Is a fixed, silent session timeout with no warning ever acceptable under WCAG?
contentSections.answer: No — not without a warning and a way to extend it. WCAG 2.2.1 Timing Adjustable (A) requires that for any time limit, the user can turn it off, adjust it, or extend it before it expires (with narrow exceptions like real-time auctions or genuinely essential limits, which a benefits application is not). A silent timeout with no warning fails this even if the *length* of the limit would otherwise be reasonable — the failure is the silence, not the duration.
contentSections.hint: The criterion isn't really about how long the timer is — think about what it requires to exist *before* the timer runs out.

contentSections.body: The two independent fixes worth naming separately in a finding, because they solve different halves of the problem: a **warning with an extend option** (a dialog at, say, two minutes remaining, offering 'Stay logged in') satisfies 2.2.1 directly, and **autosave to a draft** protects the actual content even if the warning is somehow missed — the person picks back up mid-sentence instead of from zero. A form handling something as effortful to compose as a medical history genuinely warrants both, not either.
A time limit without a warning and a way to extend it isn't a security feature — it's an unannounced way to destroy work, and WCAG 2.2.1 exists specifically to rule it out.

title: Limited attention and memory as a design constraint
description: Losing a word mid-sentence, rereading the same line three times, needing ten seconds to reorient after any interruption — limited attention and memory are a design constraint like a screen reader or a colour-blind-safe palette, and standards coverage for it is genuinely thinner than for either.

learningObjectives.text: Evaluate an interface change for whether it genuinely reduces cognitive load or only appears to
Name the specific limits of current WCAG cognitive-accessibility guidance honestly

contentSections.title: What brain fog actually does to a screen

contentSections.body: A dashboard has 14 identically-styled cards in a grid — same size, same font weight, no differentiating headings beyond a small icon. Finding the one piece of information that's actually relevant today means reading all 14, in order, because nothing about the layout tells you where to look first. For someone mid-flare, that's not an inconvenience — a lost thread mid-sentence, needing to reread the same card three times to hold onto what it said, is the baseline, not a bad day within a bad day.

contentSections.scenario: A team redesigning a benefits dashboard for 'cognitive accessibility' proposes a set of changes.
contentSections.question: Which of these genuinely reduce cognitive load for someone with brain fog? Select all that apply.

items.label: Give each of the 14 cards a distinct, specific heading instead of a shared generic label
Show exactly one primary action per screen instead of five equally-weighted buttons
Autosave form progress so nothing is lost if the person has to stop and come back
Add motion and colour animation to draw attention to the most important card
Compress five separate screens into one long scrolling page 'to reduce the number of clicks'

explanation.unique-headings: Yes — a specific heading lets someone scan for the one relevant card instead of reading all 14 in full to find it, which is exactly the difference between a chunked task and an undifferentiated one.
explanation.one-action: Yes — reducing the number of equally-weighted choices reduces what has to be evaluated and held in mind before acting, which is a direct cognitive-load reduction, not just a visual simplification.
explanation.autosave: Yes — protecting against loss from an interruption (which brain fog and fatigue make far more likely, not less) removes one whole category of catastrophic failure the person otherwise has to guard against by staying hyper-vigilant.
explanation.more-animation: No — motion and colour draw attention, but attention and cognitive load are different things; added animation is itself an extra thing to process and can be actively harmful for attention regulation, on top of the separate vestibular-symptom risk covered in the next module.
explanation.one-screen: No — this optimises for click count, which isn't the actual cost. One long screen means everything has to be held in view or in mind simultaneously, and scroll position becomes a new thing to track and lose; five short, single-purpose screens with a visible 'step 3 of 5' indicator usually cost less cognitively despite costing more clicks.

contentSections.synthesis: Three of these reduce what has to be held in mind at any one moment — a specific heading, one clear action, protection against losing work. The other two optimise for something that looks like simplicity (fewer screens, more visual guidance) while actually increasing what has to be tracked simultaneously. 'Fewer clicks' and 'less to hold in your head' are not the same metric, and a redesign that only measures the first can make the second worse.

contentSections.body: The honest limit worth stating plainly: WCAG's own Cognitive Accessibility guidance (published through the COGA task force) is largely advisory, not a set of testable Level A/AA success criteria the way keyboard operability or contrast are. Some of it — 3.3.7 Redundant Entry, 3.3.2 Labels or Instructions — has been folded into enforceable criteria over successive WCAG versions; a lot of it (plain-language guidance, help availability, avoiding interruptions) hasn't, and may never fit cleanly into a pass/fail criterion the way a contrast ratio does. That doesn't make it less real. It means an audit report has to be willing to name a cognitive barrier as a finding on its own evaluative merits, the same way this whole module has, rather than only reporting what a citation can carry.

Cognitive load affects far more people, far more of the time, than a narrow diagnosed population — pain, medication, sleep deprivation and divided attention all produce it situationally, and standards coverage for it is thinner than for almost anything else in this track.

contentSections.title: What actually helps, and what only looks like it does

contentSections.body: A 'cognitive accessibility redesign' document proposes merging a 5-step application into a single scrolling page, removing the step indicator entirely ('it added visual clutter'), and replacing all confirmation dialogs with instant auto-save-on-change ('fewer clicks, less friction').

contentSections.code:
Redesign proposal, cognitive accessibility section:

1. Merge steps 1-5 into one continuous scrolling page
2. Remove the "Step 3 of 5" progress indicator (reduces visual clutter)
3. Replace "Are you sure?" confirmation dialogs with instant auto-save on every field change
4. Simplify all button copy to single words: "Next", "Back", "Done"
contentSections.question: This document is genuinely trying to reduce cognitive load and gets at least two things backwards. Which changes actually increase it?

options.label: Only #1 — the others are all correct simplifications
#1 and #2 together — merging screens removes chunking, and removing the progress indicator removes the one thing telling someone where they are and how much is left
#3 and #4 — confirmations and full-word buttons are always better for cognitive load

feedback.one-only: The progress indicator's removal is doing real damage on its own — 'where am I, and how much is left' is exactly the kind of orienting information brain fog erodes fastest, and losing it isn't offset by anything else in this document.
feedback.one-two: Right. Merging screens removes the chunking that made each step a self-contained, completable unit, replacing it with one undifferentiated block someone has to hold in view and track scroll position within. Removing the progress indicator removes the one piece of the interface answering 'where am I, how much is left' — which matters more, not less, once everything else has been merged into a single page with no natural stopping points.
feedback.three-four: Single-word button copy (#4) is a genuine, uncomplicated improvement — shorter, clearer, no ambiguity. Instant auto-save without confirmation (#3) removes a moment some users rely on to catch a mistake before it's committed; it's a real trade-off, not an unambiguous win either way, but it isn't the clear regression #1 and #2 are.

contentSections.flawExplanation: Both #1 and #2 chase 'fewer clicks' and 'less visual clutter' as if those were the same thing as lower cognitive load. Chunking a task into discrete, completable steps — each one small enough to hold in mind and finish before moving on — is one of the most reliable real reductions in cognitive load available, and a progress indicator is what makes chunking legible to the person doing it rather than just a technical fact about the code. Removing both trades a measurable improvement for a metric (click count, pixel density) that doesn't actually track what brain fog struggles with.

contentSections.body: Brain fog isn't solved by simplifying the words on a page if the structure underneath still asks someone to hold six things in mind at once — chunking, a visible sense of progress, and protection against losing work reduce load; fewer clicks and less visual clutter often just move the load somewhere less visible.

title: Practice — Find the Cognitive Barrier in Eight Flows
description: Eight drills across the module's skills. No new concepts: this is where naming a cognitive barrier stops being something you've read about and becomes something you recognise fast.

learningObjectives.text: Apply redundant-entry, predictability and error-recovery diagnosis to unfamiliar flows at speed
Distinguish a genuine WCAG citation from an honest evaluative finding with none available

contentSections.title: Eight drills

contentSections.body: Nothing new here. Eight drills across the module's skills, ordered from where the lessons ended to one step past it. Do them in one sitting if that works, or three — the set doesn't expire and nothing is timed.
If a drill needed a hint, that's the thing to watch for in the checkpoint — not a reason to redo the set.

title: Lab — Audit a Multi-Step Form for Cognitive Load
description: Pick a real multi-step form and walk it with a specific question at every field: what does this ask me to hold in my head, and what happens to everything else if I get one thing wrong?

learningObjectives.text: Map the memory demand a real multi-step form places on its user, step by step
Test a form's error-recovery behaviour deliberately and log what a single mistake actually costs
Write specific, implementable reductions rather than a general recommendation to 'simplify'

contentSections.title: The lab

contentSections.body: Pick a real multi-step form you can access today — a job application, a benefits portal, an account signup, a booking flow. This lab produces an audit of what it demands from working memory and what a single mistake actually costs, not a redesign.

contentSections.title: Cognitive load audit of a multi-step form
contentSections.brief: Choose a real, multi-step form (at least 4 distinct steps or screens) you can access with the energy you have today. Walk it once as a normal user would, then a second time specifically hunting for redundant entry, unpredictable movement, badly-timed instructions and destructive error recovery. Deliberately trigger at least one validation error to see what it actually costs.
contentSections.deliverable: An audit naming every point of memory demand, every recovery-cost finding from a deliberate error, and a specific, concrete reduction proposed for each — not a general note to 'simplify.'

stages.title: Choose the flow and do a first pass
stages.instructions: Pick a form with at least 4 steps. Complete it once, normally, noting anywhere you had to stop and think back to an earlier screen, anywhere you weren't sure what was expected, or anywhere something moved while you were mid-interaction.
stages.checkpoint: You've named the flow, its starting point, and have a raw list of anything that gave you pause on a first honest pass.

stages.title: Map the memory demand, step by step
stages.instructions: For each step, note explicitly: does this step ask for anything already provided earlier? Is it displayed, or does the user have to recall it? Is any instruction (format, requirement) visible at the moment it's needed, or only before/after? Cite WCAG 3.3.7 or 3.3.2 wherever one genuinely applies.
stages.checkpoint: Every step has a memory-demand note, and every redundant-entry or missing-instruction case is either cited or explicitly marked as evaluative with no clean citation.

stages.title: Deliberately break it and log the recovery cost
stages.instructions: Trigger at least one real validation error (a wrong format, a required field left blank) and observe precisely: what gets cleared, does focus move to the error, is the specific field marked, is the error message specific enough to act on without guessing. Also check for any time-limited element (a session timer, a one-time code) and whether a warning and extension exist.
stages.checkpoint: You have a precise account of what one real mistake actually costs in this flow — not a guess, an observed result.

stages.title: Write reductions and self-check
stages.instructions: For every finding, write a specific, implementable change — not 'reduce cognitive load' but the actual mechanism (a checkbox to reuse an address, a persistent instruction instead of a placeholder, per-field error clearing instead of whole-form clearing). Then run the self-check below.
stages.checkpoint: Every finding has a named location, a specific cost, and a specific, implementable reduction.

rubric.criterion: Memory demand is mapped step by step, not summarised in general terms
rubric.meets: A reader can see exactly which step asks for what, and whether it was already provided earlier in the same flow.

rubric.criterion: At least one error was deliberately triggered and its real cost observed
rubric.meets: The recovery-cost finding is based on what actually happened when tested, not an assumption about what probably happens.

rubric.criterion: Citations are used only where they genuinely fit
rubric.meets: At least one finding is logged as evaluative, with no forced citation, if the flow warranted it — matching the honest-limits pattern from this module.

rubric.criterion: Every reduction is specific and implementable
rubric.meets: A developer reading only the reduction, with no further conversation, would know exactly what to build.

rubric.criterion: The audit reflects a real energy budget
rubric.meets: The stages were completed as separate sittings if needed — nothing about the audit required doing it in one unbroken 50-minute block.

contentSections.body: A form you've only ever completed correctly on the first try is a form whose actual cost to a wrong turn you don't know — this lab is the difference between assuming it's fine and having tested it.

title: Checkpoint — Cognitive Accessibility
description: Ten questions, all from this module. Each course is sold separately, so nothing here draws on other courses. Ungraded, untimed, and getting one wrong just means it comes back later.

learningObjectives.text: Retrieve this module's distinctions on working memory, consistency, instructions, error recovery and time limits, without looking them up

contentSections.title: Let's see what stuck
Checkpoint — Cognitive Accessibility

questions.from: This module — Cognitive Accessibility
questions.prompt: A billing address field is blank with no checkbox to reuse the shipping address entered earlier. What does this violate?

options.label: WCAG 3.3.7 Redundant Entry — no mechanism to reuse or auto-populate the earlier value
Nothing — the user already typed the address once
WCAG 2.1.2 No Keyboard Trap

questions.explanation: 3.3.7 requires information already provided to be auto-populated or available to select, not simply theoretically re-typeable by the user.

questions.from: This module — Cognitive Accessibility
questions.prompt: A button shifts position under a growing 'unsaved changes' banner, right as the user aims to click it. Which WCAG criterion covers this?

options.label: 3.2.2 On Input — any unexpected layout change is covered
None directly — 3.2.1/3.2.2 cover context changes like navigation or focus shifts, not layout reflow; this is a real barrier with no clean citation
1.4.3 Contrast

questions.explanation: 3.2.1/3.2.2 are scoped to context changes — navigation, new windows, focus jumps — not layout reflow. This is exactly the kind of barrier this whole phase exists to name even without a clean citation.

questions.from: This module — Cognitive Accessibility
questions.prompt: Why does blocking paste on a one-time verification code field tend to increase errors rather than reduce them?

options.label: It forces manual retention and retyping across an app switch, exactly the condition most likely to produce a transposed digit
Paste never works reliably on mobile devices anyway
It doesn't — this is a myth

questions.explanation: The failure mode blocking paste prevents is minor; the failure mode it guarantees — everyone retyping a number from memory under time pressure — is the larger one.

questions.from: This module — Cognitive Accessibility
questions.prompt: A password field's only instructions are placeholder text. What's the core problem?

options.label: Placeholder text is always too low-contrast to read
Placeholders aren't supported in most modern browsers
The placeholder disappears the moment the user starts typing, removing the instruction at exactly the point it would help

questions.explanation: A placeholder is designed to vanish on input, which guarantees it's gone right when someone would check their input against it — the fix is a persistent instruction, not removing the placeholder.

questions.from: This module — Cognitive Accessibility
questions.prompt: A form clears a CVV field after a declined payment, but also clears the correctly-entered shipping address on the same page. What's the right read?

options.label: Clearing the CVV is a defensible security choice; clearing the unrelated shipping address is a state-management defect, not a security decision
Both are defensible — any failed submission should clear all fields
Neither should ever be cleared, under any circumstances

questions.explanation: Not persisting a sensitive value like a CVV is a real, narrow security decision. Clearing unrelated fields alongside it has no equivalent justification — it's an implementation shortcut.

questions.from: This module — Cognitive Accessibility
questions.prompt: Under real-world load such as tiredness or interruption, roughly how many items does working memory reliably hold, per the lesson?

options.label: Roughly three or four items held at once
Roughly seven items, give or take two
Roughly twelve items held at the same time

questions.explanation: The lesson says working memory under load holds around three or four items, and that the often quoted 7 plus or minus 2 figure has been revised downward.

questions.from: This module — Cognitive Accessibility
questions.prompt: Which re-entry does WCAG 3.3.7 Redundant Entry leave alone on purpose?

options.label: A date of birth asked for again on each page of the form
An email address typed again on the next screen of a form
A password confirmation field that needs fresh typing

questions.explanation: Essential re-entry is carved out. A password confirmation needs an independent entry and a payment CVV should never be stored. The judgement call is whether re-entry is essential or nobody built the reuse.

questions.from: This module — Cognitive Accessibility
questions.prompt: Why does WCAG 3.2.4 Consistent Identification matter for people with limited energy?

options.label: Because it keeps brand colours the same across the whole site
Because users can act on habit instead of re-reading screens
Because it shortens each page so there is less text to read

questions.explanation: The same label and icon wherever the same thing happens means habit can carry the user. It is not about branding polish.

questions.from: This module — Cognitive Accessibility
questions.prompt: A timed form session has no warning before it logs the user out. Which two fixes does the lesson name, and why both?

options.label: A longer timeout for all users, plus a larger logout button
A warning alone, since autosave is a security risk for forms
A warning with an extend option, plus autosave for missed ones

questions.explanation: The two fixes solve different halves of the problem. A form as effortful as a long application form warrants both, not either.

questions.from: This module — Cognitive Accessibility
questions.prompt: How does the lesson say cognitive barriers should be treated when no single WCAG criterion covers them?

options.label: They are left out because they cannot be tested pass or fail
They are named as findings on their own evaluative merits
They are reported if the client asks about them directly

questions.explanation: COGA guidance is largely advisory, and a lot of it does not fit a pass or fail criterion. That does not make it less real, so the report names the barrier anyway.

contentSections.body: None of these need to be perfect. What matters is which ones needed a guess — that's what the next checkpoint will bring back.

title: Plain language that isn't patronising
description: Plain language is a rewrite of how something is said, not a permission slip to say less — a rewrite that removes the reason a claim was denied is not more accessible than the dense original, it's just shorter.

learningObjectives.text: Distinguish genuine plain-language simplification from oversimplification that removes necessary meaning
Apply WCAG 3.1.5 Reading Level to real interface copy, including its practical limits
Identify when a 'simplified' rewrite is actually patronising rather than clearer

contentSections.title: Plain language is not baby talk

contentSections.body: A benefits agency's denial letter reads: 'Your claim was not approved because you did not satisfy the continuous residency requirement for the qualifying period under Regulation 14(3).' A rewrite team produces two alternatives. Version A: 'We couldn't approve your claim because our records show a gap in your residency during the period we're required to check (Regulation 14(3) has the exact rule). If this looks wrong, you can send us proof of where you lived during that time.' Version B: 'Sorry, this didn't work out! Feel free to try again another time.'

contentSections.scenario: Version A keeps the specific reason and a concrete next step, in plain sentences. Version B is friendlier and shorter, and states neither.
contentSections.question: Which version is genuinely plain language, and which one just looks simpler?

options.label: Version B — it's shorter and has no jargon at all
Version A — it keeps the actual reason and the actual next step, in plain words; Version B deletes the information the person needs to act
Both are equally good — either reads easier than the original

feedback.b: Shorter isn't the test. Version B is pleasant to read but has deleted the one thing the reader actually needs — why the claim failed and what they can do next — which makes it useless to act on, not more accessible.
feedback.a: Right. Version A keeps everything Version B threw away — the actual reason (a residency gap), where the rule lives, and a concrete next step — and states all of it in plain sentences. Plain language means stating necessary complexity clearly, not deleting it.
feedback.both: Version B reads easier at a glance, but 'easier to read' and 'useful to the person reading it' are different measurements — B gives someone nothing to actually act on.

contentSections.concept: **Plain language rewrites how something is said, not whether it needs saying at all.** The dense original and Version B fail in opposite directions — one buries the reason in legal phrasing, the other deletes the reason entirely — and a rewrite that trades one failure for the other hasn't made the letter more accessible, just differently useless. The actual job is finding the plainest sentence that still contains everything the reader needs to act.

contentSections.body: **WCAG 3.1.5 Reading Level (AAA)** requires a supplemental version, or the text itself, not to demand reading ability beyond lower-secondary education — unless the content genuinely can't be simplified further without losing meaning, or a plain-language version is provided alongside the original. That exception matters as much as the rule: a clinical trial consent form can't legally omit certain terms, and a mortgage agreement can't quietly drop a clause because it's hard to phrase simply. The job in those cases isn't deleting the hard part, it's finding the plainest *true* version and, where the content genuinely can't get simpler, supplementing it rather than replacing it.

It's also worth being honest about 3.1.5's practical weight: it's an AAA criterion, which almost no organisation formally commits to meeting, and 'lower-secondary reading level' isn't mechanically testable the way a contrast ratio is — nobody runs a script and gets a pass/fail. That doesn't make plain language optional or unauditable. It means an audit names plain-language failures as evaluative findings, the same honest pattern the previous module used for layout shift and brain fog: real, specific, and worth reporting, whether or not a single AAA citation covers it cleanly.
Plain language means saying necessary complexity clearly, not saying less — a rewrite that deletes the reason or the next step has traded one failure for another, not fixed it.

contentSections.title: Where the actual editing work happens

contentSections.body: An insurance policy reads: 'In the event of a Qualifying Life Event, Enrollees must submit documentation substantiating eligibility within thirty (30) calendar days of the Event Date, absent which coverage modifications shall not be effected retroactively.' Every individual word here is ordinary. The sentence is still genuinely hard to parse.

contentSections.scenario: The sentence above has almost no jargon — 'documentation,' 'eligibility,' 'coverage' are all common words. It's still difficult to follow on a first read.
contentSections.question: What's actually making this sentence hard, if not the vocabulary?

options.label: The individual words are too advanced for a general reader
Nominalised verbs (documentation substantiating eligibility, instead of 'prove you qualify'), a passive final clause, and one long conditional sentence carrying three separate rules at once
It isn't actually hard — this reads fine once you're used to policy documents

feedback.words: Word-by-word, almost everything here is common vocabulary — 'documentation,' 'eligibility,' 'coverage' would all pass a jargon check individually. The difficulty is coming from somewhere else entirely.
feedback.structure: Right. This sentence stacks a formal trigger clause ('In the event of a Qualifying Life Event'), a buried verb turned into a noun ('documentation substantiating eligibility' instead of the plain 'prove you qualify'), and a passive negative conditional ('absent which... shall not be effected') into one 40-word sentence carrying three separate rules — deadline, requirement, and consequence — with no visual separation between them.
feedback.denial: Familiarity can make dense prose feel normal to someone who reads a lot of it, which is exactly the trap — the person this letter is actually for is reading it for the first time, at the worst possible moment to be untangling three rules from one sentence.

contentSections.mechanism: **Reading difficulty usually comes from sentence structure and buried verbs, not big words.** Nominalisations turn actions into nouns — 'documentation substantiating eligibility' instead of 'prove you qualify' — which forces a reader to reconstruct the actual verb before they can follow what's happening. Stacking a trigger, a requirement, a deadline and a consequence into one sentence forces all four to be held in mind simultaneously before any of them resolves. The fix is structural: one rule per sentence, active voice, the verb stated plainly.

contentSections.body: This is exactly why an automated reading-level score can mislead on its own, which the next lesson in this module covers directly: a tool measuring syllables and sentence length would flag this sentence as difficult mainly for its length, and a lazy fix — just splitting it at the commas — would still leave the nominalisations and the passive clause intact. A genuine rewrite finds the plain verb first ('Tell us within 30 days if your situation changes') and builds the sentence around it, rather than mechanically shortening the original.
Ordinary words in a badly-structured sentence are still hard to read — the fix is finding the buried verb and giving each rule its own sentence, not swapping words for shorter synonyms.

title: Link text, button text and "click here"
description: Ten identical 'Read more' links defeat the one navigation method a lot of screen reader users reach for first — pulling a list of every link on the page — even on a page where sighted context makes each one obvious.

learningObjectives.text: Apply WCAG 2.4.4 Link Purpose (In Context) to link text that depends on surrounding text
Explain why WCAG 2.4.9 Link Purpose (Link Only) matters in practice even though it's AAA
Identify duplicate or generic control labels that break navigation by link or button list

contentSections.title: Link text that only works with eyes on the paragraph around it

contentSections.body: A news site's homepage lists ten story teasers, each ending in a link reading 'Read more.' A screen reader user pulls up the page's link list — the fast way to see everything a page links to without reading the whole thing — and hears 'Read more, Read more, Read more' ten times in a row, with no way to tell one from another.

contentSections.scenario: Version 1: every teaser ends in a link that just says 'Read more.' Version 2: every teaser ends in a link that says 'Read more about the flood warning for Cardiff' (or whichever headline it belongs to).
contentSections.question: How do these two versions compare under WCAG 2.4.4 (A) and 2.4.9 (AAA)?

options.label: Both fail — 'Read more' appearing anywhere in a link automatically fails both criteria
Version 1 can pass 2.4.4 if the surrounding paragraph disambiguates it, but fails 2.4.9 in a link-only list; Version 2 passes both because the destination is named inside the link text itself
Neither matters, because a sighted user can already tell which story each link belongs to from the layout

feedback.bothfail: 2.4.4 explicitly allows link purpose to be determined from context — the link text plus its enclosing sentence, list item, or table cell — so 'Read more' inside a specific, differentiated paragraph can genuinely satisfy it. The two criteria test different things, and this option collapses them into one.
feedback.distinguish: Right. 2.4.4 is satisfied by link text plus programmatically-associated context (the paragraph it sits in). 2.4.9 removes that allowance entirely — link text has to stand alone. Version 1 relies on context that a link-list view strips away; Version 2 doesn't need the context at all because the destination is stated inside the link.
feedback.sightedonly: The whole reason 2.4.4/2.4.9 exist is that link purpose has to be determinable without relying on layout or visual proximity — a sighted user's ability to eyeball which teaser a link belongs to says nothing about whether a screen reader user, navigating by link list with none of that visual layout present, can tell the same thing.

contentSections.concept: **2.4.4 and 2.4.9 test the same idea at two different strictness levels.** 2.4.4 (A) allows link purpose to be determined from the link text combined with its immediate context — the sentence or list item it's inside. 2.4.9 (AAA) requires the link text alone, with no context at all, to be enough — because a link-list or rotor view genuinely strips every bit of surrounding context away and shows nothing but the links themselves.

contentSections.body: This matters more in practice than the AAA label suggests. Pulling a link list — or a heading list, or an elements list — is one of the fastest ways many screen reader users get a sense of a page before reading it in full, exactly the navigation pattern from the assistive-tech phase's rotor and elements-list lesson. Ten identical 'Read more' links defeats that entire method, even on a page where 2.4.4 technically passes because each link sits in a differentiated paragraph. A good audit names this as a real usability finding worth fixing, not just a nice-to-have, even where the formal citation available is the AAA one.

'Read more' can pass 2.4.4 inside a specific paragraph and still defeat link-list navigation completely — 2.4.9 exists because context a sighted reader relies on is exactly what a link list strips away.

contentSections.title: Buttons with the same name, meaning different things

contentSections.body: A subscriptions page lists five plans in a table, each row ending in a button that reads 'Cancel.' The visible text is identical five times over. A screen reader user pulling up a button list hears 'Cancel, Cancel, Cancel, Cancel, Cancel' with no way to tell which plan each one cancels.

contentSections.question: Does a table of five identical 'Cancel' buttons meet WCAG 2.4.4, given each row's plan name is visible in the same table row?
contentSections.answer: Not automatically. 2.4.4 allows purpose to be determined from context, but that context has to be programmatically available to assistive tech, not just visually present in the same row. Plain visible text 'Cancel' repeated five times, with nothing tying each button's accessible name to its row, still fails — the fix is giving each button a distinct accessible name (an aria-label like 'Cancel Premium plan', or visually-hidden text appended to the visible label) so the row context travels with the control instead of staying only on screen.
contentSections.hint: Ask specifically what a screen reader announces for the button in isolation, not what a sighted person sitting in front of the table can work out.

contentSections.body: The fix costs almost nothing: `` or an `aria-label` carrying the same disambiguating text. Sighted users see 'Cancel' exactly as before — nothing changes visually — and a screen reader announces 'Cancel Premium plan,' which is enough on its own with no table structure needed to interpret it. This is the same underlying pattern as the review-screen finding from the previous module: the information a control needs already exists on the page, it just isn't attached to the control itself.

Five identical 'Cancel' buttons look fine in a visual table and fail completely as soon as they're pulled out of it — the accessible name has to carry its own disambiguating context, not borrow it from the row around it.

title: Error messages that say what to do next
description: 'Invalid password' technically puts text near a failed field and still tells the person nothing they can act on — the difference between a compliant-looking error and a useful one is almost entirely in the wording, not the placement.

learningObjectives.text: Rewrite a vague error message into a specific, actionable one
Apply WCAG 3.3.3 Error Suggestion to the wording of a message, not just its placement
Identify blame-framed error language and rewrite it toward the system that produced it

contentSections.title: "Invalid input" is not information

contentSections.body: A signup form rejects a password with the message 'Invalid password' shown in red beneath the field. No rule is stated anywhere on the page. The field is cleared. The person now has to guess which of several possible rules — length, a number, a symbol, no spaces — they broke, and retype a password they no longer remember exactly, hoping to hit whatever the hidden rule actually is.

contentSections.scenario: The previous module covered where an error appears and whether focus moves to it. 'Invalid password' is correctly placed right next to the field and does move focus there — and the finding is still real.
contentSections.question: Given placement and focus are both already correct, what's actually still broken here?

options.label: Nothing — placement and focus were the whole requirement, and both are met

The message identifies that something is wrong without stating what the actual rule is or which part failed, so an auditor checking only 'is there text near the field' can wrongly mark this as passing
The text needs to be a different color to be noticed

feedback.nothing: Placement and focus solve the *finding* the error problem — this scenario is about what happens next, once the person has found it and still doesn't know what it's asking for.
feedback.content: Right. 3.3.1 (Error Identification) and 3.3.3 (Error Suggestion) are both worded around content, not just position — 'invalid password' identifies that an error exists but suggests nothing about how to fix it. A review that only checks placement and focus movement will mark this compliant, because it's checking the wrong half of the criteria.
feedback.color: Contrast could be its own separate, real finding, but it isn't the mechanism behind the message giving the reader nothing to act on — a bright red 'Invalid password' is exactly as unhelpful as a pale one.

contentSections.mechanism: **A message can be perfectly placed and still fail 3.3.3, because placement and content are two separate obligations.** 3.3.1 requires the item in error to be identified in text. 3.3.3 requires that, where a fix is knowable, the suggestion is provided. 'Invalid password' technically satisfies the letter of 3.3.1 — something is identified — while failing 3.3.3 outright, because no suggestion exists anywhere. The rewrite: 'Your password needs at least one number — you entered 6 characters with no numbers,' names the specific rule that failed and what to do about it.

contentSections.body: The rewriting method, stated plainly: name the field, name the specific rule that failed (not the full list of every rule, just the one actually broken, if that's determinable), state what to do. 'Enter your email in the format name@example.com — we couldn't find the @ symbol in what you typed' does all three in one sentence. A field that fails multiple rules at once can list all of them, but the pattern stays the same: specific rule, specific fix, no vague catch-all phrase standing in for either.
A message can be correctly placed and still say nothing — 3.3.3 requires the actual suggestion, and a rewrite that names the specific broken rule and the specific fix is what closes the gap.

contentSections.title: "You entered this wrong" — and the blame it carries

contentSections.body: A banking app's PIN entry reads: 'You entered an incorrect PIN. This is your last attempt before your card is locked.' The message blames the person for the mistake and states the consequence as something close to a threat, in the same sentence as the correction.

contentSections.question: Put these in the order a well-constructed error message actually states its parts.
steps: Say what's wrong, without framing it as the user's fault for a rule they had no way to see in advance
State the specific rule or format that was expected
Say exactly what to do next
If there's a real consequence, state it factually, once, without repeating it as a warning
contentSections.explanation: Leading with blame ('you entered this wrong') puts the reader on the defensive before they've even learned what the actual rule is, which is exactly backwards for a message whose whole job is helping someone fix something fast. Stating the rule and the fix before any consequence means the useful information lands first, whether or not the reader keeps reading to the end. A real consequence — a lockout, an expired session — deserves to be named factually once; restating it as a threat ('this is your LAST attempt') adds pressure without adding information, and pressure is exactly what degrades performance for someone already stressed by a failed attempt.

contentSections.body: One honest caveat worth naming directly, because it will come up in a real review: some login errors deliberately say 'incorrect email or password' without specifying which one failed, and that vagueness is a legitimate, deliberate security decision — it prevents an attacker from using the error message to enumerate which email addresses have accounts. That's a real, named trade-off, the same shape as the paste-blocking caveat from the previous module: worth stating as a trade-off in a finding, not treated as an oversight or rewritten away without checking whether the vagueness is actually protecting something.

Leading with blame delays the useful information and adds pressure that doesn't help anyone act faster — state the rule and the fix first, and save any real consequence for one factual sentence, not a repeated warning.

title: Reading level, jargon and the audience you actually have
description: A word like 'adjudication' is plain language inside a claims department and genuine jargon to a first-time claimant — jargon is relative to who's actually reading, not a fixed list of hard words, and a readability score can't tell the difference.

learningObjectives.text: Evaluate interface copy against the audience that actually uses the product, not an assumed one
Identify jargon that reads as plain to the person who wrote it
State the specific limits of automated readability scores

contentSections.title: The audience in the room when the copy was written, versus the audience reading it

contentSections.body: A patient portal shows a lab result: 'Your recent lipid panel indicates mild dyslipidemia; consult your PCP regarding statin therapy initiation.' It was reviewed and approved by two clinicians, for whom every word here is completely ordinary. The person reading it just opened an app on their phone, alone, right after getting a result they don't yet understand.

contentSections.scenario: A team redesigning that result page for clarity proposes several changes.
contentSections.question: Which of these genuinely make the result understandable to the actual reader? Select all that apply.

items.label: Define 'dyslipidemia' in plain words the first time it appears, then keep using the same word consistently afterward
Replace 'PCP' with 'your regular doctor'
Add a one-line plain-language summary of what the result means at the top of the page, before the clinical detail
Run the whole page through an automated text-simplifier tool and publish the output without clinical review
Remove the specific numeric values entirely, 'to avoid alarming patients'

explanation.define-once: Yes — defining a necessary clinical term once, in plain words, keeps the precision the term carries while making it usable by someone meeting it for the first time. This is the 3.1.5 exception working as intended: the word stays because it's genuinely needed, and a plain-language bridge is added alongside it.
explanation.pcp: Yes — 'PCP' is an internal abbreviation with zero value to the reader and a real cost: someone unfamiliar with it either has to guess or stop and look it up at the exact moment they're trying to understand a health result.
explanation.summary-first: Yes — leading with what the result actually means, in plain words, respects that most readers want the takeaway before the clinical detail, and gives anyone who stops reading after one line the information that matters most.
explanation.auto-simplify: No — an automated simplifier can shorten sentences and swap in common synonyms, but it has no way to verify the output is still clinically accurate; publishing unreviewed simplified medical text risks introducing a wrong or misleading statement in the name of clarity, which is a worse failure than the jargon it replaced.
explanation.strip-numbers: No — the actual number is often the one thing a patient specifically wants (their own value, not just a category label), and removing it doesn't reduce alarm, it removes information and replaces a real number with an unexplained gap, which tends to increase anxiety rather than lower it.

contentSections.synthesis: Three of these keep the necessary information and change how it's presented — a definition, a plain substitute for an internal abbreviation, a summary that leads with meaning. The other two look like simplification but actually remove real content: an unreviewed auto-simplified page risks clinical accuracy for the sake of a shorter sentence, and stripping numbers removes exactly the specific fact a patient is looking for. 'Simpler' and 'less information' aren't the same goal, and a redesign that only optimises the first can quietly fail the second.

contentSections.body: The honest limit worth stating directly: automated readability scores like Flesch-Kincaid measure sentence length and syllable count. They cannot detect jargon that happens to be short — 'PCP,' 'statin,' 'afib' all score as easy words by syllable count alone — and they cannot tell whether a passing score was achieved by genuinely clarifying a sentence or by quietly deleting the hard part of it. A passing readability score is a useful, necessary signal. It is not sufficient evidence that the content is actually clear to the real reader, and a rewrite that chases the score without checking against real jargon and real deletions can pass the metric while failing the person.
A readability score measures sentence length and syllables, not jargon or deleted meaning — passing the score is necessary, not sufficient, evidence that the content is actually clear.

contentSections.title: Jargon that the writer can't see anymore

contentSections.body: A claims team ships a 'plain language pass' on their denial letters. The letters are shorter now, and still full of 'adjudication,' 'means-tested' and 'co-payment,' used with no definition anywhere — because inside the claims department, none of those words register as jargon at all. Nobody flagged them.

contentSections.question: Is a word 'jargon' because it's technically a specialised term, or because of who's expected to already know it?
contentSections.answer: Because of who's expected to already know it. Jargon is relative to the actual audience, not a fixed list of difficult-sounding words — 'adjudication' is completely ordinary inside a claims department and genuine jargon to a first-time claimant reading a denial letter alone. The real test is never 'does this word sound technical,' it's 'would the actual person reading this, right now, already know it' — and a writer who uses a term daily is the person least able to answer that question by instinct.
contentSections.hint: Think about why the claims team didn't catch their own jargon even while deliberately doing a 'plain language pass' — what would they have needed that they didn't have?

contentSections.body: The practical fix is process, not vocabulary: test copy with someone who genuinely isn't a subject-matter expert, before it ships — not a colleague from an adjacent team who's also fluent in the jargon, an actual outsider. A second, cheaper method: keep a running list of terms drawn from real support tickets asking 'what does this mean,' since that list is a direct, ongoing signal of exactly which words the internal team has stopped noticing as jargon, updated by the audience itself rather than guessed at.

The person who uses a term every day is the worst-positioned person to notice it's jargon — testing with a genuine outsider, or tracking real 'what does this mean' support tickets, catches what a self-review never will.

title: Alt text: what to write when the image carries meaning
description: A purely decorative photo, a data-bearing chart, an icon-only button and a product photo a shopper actually needs all want different alt text — and the single most common real-world error is treating all four the same way.

learningObjectives.text: Classify an image as decorative, informative, functional or complex before writing its alt text
Apply WCAG 1.1.1 to write alt text sized to what the image actually communicates
Identify over-description that adds screen reader burden without adding meaning

contentSections.title: Four kinds of image, four different answers

contentSections.body: A product page has four images: a full-width brand hero photo with no unique information, an image of a size chart with numbers that exist nowhere else on the page, an icon-only button that downloads a spec sheet PDF, and a product photo showing the actual colour and cut a shopper needs to judge before buying.

contentSections.intro: Classify each image before deciding what its alt text should carry.

fields.prompt: The full-width brand hero photo — purely visual, adds no information not already stated elsewhere on the page.

options.label: Decorative — empty alt (alt="")
Informative — describe everything visible
Complex — provide the underlying data as text

feedback.decorative: Right. Nothing here is information the page doesn't already state elsewhere — an empty alt (still a real, required attribute, alt="", not a missing one) tells assistive tech to skip it entirely rather than announce something with no content.
feedback.informative: Describing a purely decorative image in detail adds listening time for exactly zero information — the test for 'informative' is whether the image conveys something the surrounding page doesn't already say.
feedback.complex: There's no underlying data here to reproduce — this classification is for charts, graphs and diagrams, not brand photography.

fields.prompt: An image of a size table — measurements that exist only inside the image, nowhere else on the page as real text.

options.label: Decorative — empty alt
Complex — the image needs its actual data reproduced as real text or an HTML table, not just described
Functional — describe the action it performs

feedback.decorative: This image is the only place the size data exists on the page — treating it as decorative would delete real information a shopper needs to make a purchase decision.
feedback.complex: Right. A caption or a short alt like 'size chart' identifies that a chart exists without giving anyone the actual measurements. Complex images need their real content — here, an HTML table with the same numbers — provided as an equivalent, not just labelled.
feedback.functional: This image doesn't perform an action, it displays data — functional classification is for controls like buttons or links rendered as an image.

fields.prompt: An icon-only button — a small download-arrow glyph, no visible text — that downloads a spec sheet PDF.

options.label: Functional — the alt text (or aria-label) should describe the action, not the icon's appearance
Decorative — empty alt
Informative — describe the arrow shape and colour

feedback.functional: Right. A functional image is a control — the alt text's job is naming what activating it does ('Download spec sheet (PDF)'), not what the icon visually looks like. 'Downward arrow icon' tells a screen reader user nothing about what pressing the button actually does.
feedback.decorative: An empty alt here would leave the button with no accessible name at all — this is a real interactive control, not a purely visual flourish, and it fails 4.1.2 (Name, Role, Value) if the name is missing.
feedback.informative: Describing the icon's shape ('a downward arrow') answers the wrong question — what matters is the action the button performs, not what the glyph looks like.

fields.prompt: A product photo showing the actual colour and cut a shopper is deciding between.

options.label: Informative — describe what a sighted user would actually learn from looking at it (colour, style, relevant detail)
Decorative — empty alt
Complex — provide the full pixel-level detail as text

feedback.informative: Right. This image is doing real work a sighted shopper relies on — the alt text should convey the same purchasing-relevant information: 'Navy blue crew-neck sweater, ribbed cuffs and hem,' not every visual detail, just what actually informs the decision.
feedback.decorative: This image is carrying real information the surrounding product page text may not fully state — the exact colour and cut a shopper is choosing between — so treating it as decorative deletes information someone needs.
feedback.complex: Complex treatment (full data reproduction) is for charts and diagrams where the image *is* the data — a product photo needs a description sized to what a sighted glance actually tells a shopper, not an exhaustive visual transcript.

contentSections.synthesis: Four different jobs get four different answers: decorative gets empty alt so it's skipped entirely; functional describes the action a control performs, not its appearance; informative describes what a sighted user would actually learn, sized to what matters; complex needs the real underlying data reproduced as text, not just labelled as existing. The single most common real error is collapsing the second and third distinction — treating a functional icon like a decoration, or an informative photo like a decoration — because both mistakes look, at a glance, like 'this image doesn't need a real description.'

contentSections.body: **WCAG 1.1.1 Non-text Content (A)** requires a text alternative that serves the same purpose as the image, for every non-text element. The size-chart case is worth specific attention because it's a widespread real failure: an image of tabular data can never be fully replaced by alt text, because alt text is a single string, not a table — the actual fix is publishing the real data as an HTML table (or plain text) somewhere on the page, with the image either removed or kept as a visual supplement to text that already carries the real content.
Decorative, informative, functional, complex — four different jobs, four different answers, and the most common real mistake is treating a functional or informative image like a decoration.

contentSections.title: The alt text that says too much

contentSections.body: Next to an 'About Us' paragraph that has nothing to do with any specific person's appearance, a conscientious editor writes: alt="A photograph of a smiling woman with brown hair wearing a blue cardigan, sitting at a wooden table with a laptop open in front of her, natural light coming through a window on the left, a small plant visible on the windowsill, holding a white ceramic mug." The photo is stock imagery, purely illustrative.

contentSections.code: alt="A photograph of a smiling woman with brown hair wearing a blue cardigan, sitting at a wooden table with a laptop open in front of her, natural light coming through a window on the left, a small plant visible on the windowsill, holding a white ceramic mug"
contentSections.question: What's actually wrong with this alt text?

options.label: It over-describes a loosely illustrative image, forcing a screen reader user to sit through a long paragraph for an image that conveys nothing the surrounding page doesn't already say
Nothing — more detail in alt text is always more accessible
It should additionally describe the woman's ethnicity, for completeness

feedback.overdesc: Right. Alt text length should match how much the image actually contributes to the page's meaning. A sighted user skims past a stock photo like this in well under a second; a screen reader user has to sit through the entire alt text read aloud, word for word, with no equivalent skim option — so verbosity here is a real, measurable listening-time cost, not evidence of thoroughness.
feedback.moreisbetter: More detail is only useful if the image is actually carrying that much meaning. For a decorative or loosely illustrative photo, exhaustive detail adds listening time without adding anything a reader needs — it's the audio equivalent of forcing someone to read a full paragraph before they're allowed to continue.
