feedback.ethnicity: Adding more physical detail makes the actual problem worse, not better — the image isn't illustrating anything that requires a physical description at all here, so the more relevant question is whether it needs any content-carrying alt text beyond a brief functional description, or none.

contentSections.flawExplanation: This image is either purely decorative (if it's not illustrating anything specific the 'About Us' text discusses) or, at most, loosely informative and deserves a one-line functional description like 'A person working at a laptop' — not a full visual transcript. The right question before writing any alt text is always 'what does this image actually contribute to someone who can't see it,' and the answer here is very little, which should produce very little alt text, not an exhaustive one.

contentSections.body: Alt text length should track how much an image actually contributes, not how conscientious the writer wants to appear — a decorative photo described in a full paragraph costs a screen reader user real listening time for no real information.

title: Practice — Rewrite Eight Pieces of Interface Copy
description: Eight drills across the module's skills. No new concepts: this is where telling genuine plain language from oversimplification, and a useful error message from a vague one, stops being something you've read about.

learningObjectives.text: Apply plain-language, link-text, error-message and alt-text judgement to unfamiliar copy at speed
Distinguish real simplification from deletion of necessary meaning

contentSections.title: Eight drills

contentSections.body: Nothing new here. Eight drills across the module's skills, ordered from where the lessons ended to one step past it. Do them in one sitting if that works, or spread across several — the set doesn't expire and nothing is timed.
If a drill needed a hint, that's the thing to watch for in the checkpoint — not a reason to redo the set.

title: Lab — Rewrite the Content of One Complete Flow
description: Pick a real flow and rewrite every piece of its copy with a specific test at each one: does this still say everything the reader needs, in words the actual reader would use?

learningObjectives.text: Evaluate a real flow's copy for plain language, link/button text and error-message quality
Rewrite interface copy that keeps necessary meaning while removing unnecessary difficulty
Justify each content change against a specific criterion or audience test, not general taste

contentSections.title: The lab

contentSections.body: Pick a real flow you can access today with the copy you have energy for — a signup form, a support ticket flow, an account-settings page, a checkout. This lab produces a rewritten version of its content with the reasoning for each change, not a redesign of its layout.

contentSections.title: Content rewrite of one complete flow
contentSections.brief: Choose a real flow (at least 3 distinct screens or states) you can access with the energy you have today. Walk it once noting every piece of copy that made you stop, guess, or reread — link and button text, error messages, instructions, alt text. Rewrite each one, and write down why the rewrite is better than the original, tied to a specific test from this module rather than a general impression.
contentSections.deliverable: A rewritten flow with before-and-after copy for every flagged piece of text, and the specific reasoning per change.

stages.title: Walk the flow and flag the copy
stages.instructions: Complete the flow once, noting every piece of text that required rereading, guessing, or that gave you no clear next step — headings, link and button text, instructions, error messages, alt text on meaningful images. Don't fix anything yet, just flag it with a one-line note on what's wrong.
stages.checkpoint: You have a raw list of flagged copy across the whole flow, each with a short note on what's actually wrong with it.

stages.title: Rewrite the plain-language and jargon cases
stages.instructions: For every flagged instruction, heading or body copy, write a rewrite that keeps every piece of necessary information while removing unnecessary structural difficulty (buried verbs, stacked clauses, undefined jargon). Where a term is genuinely necessary, define it once rather than deleting it.
stages.checkpoint: Every plain-language finding has a before/after pair, and nothing that was actually necessary information got deleted in the rewrite.

stages.title: Rewrite links, buttons, errors and alt text; self-check
stages.instructions: Rewrite every generic link or button label so its purpose is determinable from its own text where reasonably possible. Rewrite every vague error message to name the specific rule and the specific fix. Classify and rewrite alt text on any meaningful image (decorative, informative, functional or complex). Then run the self-check below.
stages.checkpoint: Every finding has a specific before, a specific after, and a stated reason tied to a concrete test from this module — not a general note to 'make it clearer.'

rubric.criterion: Every rewrite keeps the necessary information the original carried
rubric.meets: A reader comparing before and after can see nothing important was deleted, only restructured or clarified.

rubric.criterion: Link and button text is judged against context-dependent versus context-free purpose
rubric.meets: At least one finding explicitly notes whether it would survive being pulled into a link-only list.

rubric.criterion: Error message rewrites name a specific rule and a specific fix, not a general restatement
rubric.meets: A reader with no other context could act on the rewritten message alone.

rubric.criterion: Alt text is classified before being rewritten
rubric.meets: Each meaningful image's rewrite states which of the four categories it belongs to and why.

rubric.criterion: The work reflects a real energy budget
rubric.meets: The stages were completed as separate sittings if needed — nothing about the lab required one unbroken 50-minute block.

contentSections.body: Copy you've only ever read as its author is copy whose actual cost to a first-time reader you don't know — this lab is the difference between assuming it's clear and having tested it against a real, specific standard.

title: Checkpoint — Content, Language and Reading
description: Ten questions: five from this module and five from the module before it in this course. Nothing is drawn from other courses. Ungraded, untimed, and getting one wrong just means it comes back later.

learningObjectives.text: Retrieve this module's content and language distinctions alongside the previous module's cognitive load distinctions, without looking them up

contentSections.title: Let's see what stuck
Checkpoint — Content, Language and Reading

questions.from: This module — Content, Language and Reading
questions.prompt: A denial letter's plain-language rewrite is shorter and friendlier than the original but no longer states the actual reason for the denial. What's the right read?

options.label: It's a genuine improvement — shorter and friendlier is always more accessible
It's not real plain language — it deleted the information the reader needs to act, which is a different failure from the dense original, not a fix for it
It's fine as long as it passes an automated readability score

questions.explanation: Plain language means stating necessary complexity clearly, not deleting it — a rewrite that removes the actual reason has traded one failure (hard to read) for another (nothing to act on), not solved the original problem.

questions.from: This module — Content, Language and Reading
questions.prompt: Ten 'Read more' links, each inside a paragraph that names a different headline, might pass WCAG 2.4.4. Why can this still be a real problem worth flagging?

options.label: It isn't a problem — if 2.4.4 passes, nothing further needs checking
A link-list view strips away the surrounding paragraph entirely, so ten identical link texts defeat that whole navigation method even where in-context purpose is technically determinable
'Read more' always fails 2.4.4 regardless of context

questions.explanation: 2.4.9 (AAA) exists specifically because a link list removes all surrounding context — passing the more lenient 2.4.4 doesn't mean link-list navigation still works, and a good audit names that gap even without a mandatory citation.

questions.from: This module — Content, Language and Reading
questions.prompt: An error message reads 'Invalid password,' correctly placed next to the field with focus moved to it. Why is this still an incomplete finding?

options.label: Placement and focus are the only requirements, so this is compliant
It identifies that something is wrong (3.3.1) but suggests no actual fix (3.3.3) — the content, not just the position, has to name the rule and the fix
The text needs a different color

questions.explanation: 3.3.1 and 3.3.3 both concern content, not only placement — a technically well-placed message that names no specific rule still fails to suggest an actual fix.

questions.from: This module — Content, Language and Reading
questions.prompt: A word like 'adjudication' is unremarkable inside a claims team's internal documents. What makes it jargon in a denial letter?

options.label: Jargon is a fixed list of technical-sounding words, independent of audience
Jargon is relative to whether the actual reader is expected to already know the word — the same term can be ordinary in one context and genuine jargon in another
A word only counts as jargon once it fails an automated readability score

questions.explanation: The test is always whether the actual audience already knows the term, not whether it sounds technical — which is exactly why the person who uses a word daily is worst-placed to notice it's jargon to someone else.

questions.from: Previous module — Cognitive Accessibility
questions.prompt: Under real-world load such as tiredness or interruption, roughly how many items does working memory reliably hold, per the lesson?

options.label: Roughly seven items, give or take two
Roughly twelve items held at the same time
Roughly three or four items held at once

questions.explanation: The lesson says working memory under load holds around three or four items, and that the often quoted 7 plus or minus 2 figure has been revised downward.

questions.from: Previous module — Cognitive Accessibility
questions.prompt: Why does WCAG 3.2.4 Consistent Identification matter for people with limited energy?

options.label: Because users can act on habit instead of re-reading screens
Because it keeps brand colours the same across the whole site
Because it shortens each page so there is less text to read

questions.explanation: The same label and icon wherever the same thing happens means habit can carry the user. It is not about branding polish.

questions.from: Previous module — Cognitive Accessibility
questions.prompt: A form clears every field, not just the failed one, after a single validation error. What's the right read?

options.label: This is always a security best practice
Clearing an unrelated, correctly-entered field alongside the one that actually failed is a state-management defect, not a deliberate choice
This is only a problem if the form has fewer than five fields

questions.explanation: A narrow security reason can justify not retaining a specific sensitive value; it never justifies clearing unrelated correct fields alongside it.

questions.from: Previous module — Cognitive Accessibility
questions.prompt: A button shifts position under a growing 'unsaved changes' banner, right as the user aims to click it. Which WCAG criterion covers this?

options.label: 3.2.2 On Input, since it covers unexpected layout changes on the page
1.4.3 Contrast Minimum, since the shifted button changes its contrast
None directly, as 3.2.1 and 3.2.2 cover context changes, not reflow

questions.explanation: 3.2.1 and 3.2.2 are scoped to context changes such as navigation, new windows and focus jumps, not layout reflow. This is a real barrier with no clean citation, which is exactly the kind of barrier this whole phase exists to name.

questions.from: Previous module — Cognitive Accessibility
questions.prompt: A password field's only instructions are placeholder text. What's the core problem?

options.label: It vanishes when typing starts, just when it would help
It is rendered in low contrast, which makes it hard to read
It is missing from most of the modern browsers people use

questions.explanation: A placeholder is designed to vanish on input, so it is gone right when someone would check their input against it. The fix is a persistent instruction, not removing the placeholder.

questions.from: This module — Content, Language and Reading
questions.prompt: A size chart is published only as an image of a table. What is the real fix?

options.label: Write a long alt text that reads the table out cell by cell
Publish the data as an HTML table or text, not as alt text
Mark the image as decorative so that screen readers skip it

questions.explanation: An image of tabular data can never be fully replaced by alt text. The real data should sit on the page as a table or text, with the image kept as a supplement if wanted.

contentSections.body: None of these need to be perfect. What matters is which ones needed a guess — that's what the next checkpoint will bring back.

title: Animation, vestibular symptoms and reduced-motion preferences
description: Parallax scrolling isn't just a taste in web design for someone with a vestibular disorder — it's a real trigger for dizziness and nausea, and the fix most teams half-implement, prefers-reduced-motion, has to be scoped correctly to actually work.

learningObjectives.text: Apply WCAG 2.3.3 Animation from Interactions to interaction-triggered motion
Diagnose an over-broad prefers-reduced-motion implementation that removes essential motion along with decorative motion
Distinguish essential motion from decorative motion in a real interface

contentSections.title: Motion that's a design choice, not a system status

contentSections.body: A real-estate site's listing page uses parallax scrolling — background images move at a different speed than foreground content as the user scrolls. For most visitors it reads as polish. For someone with a vestibular disorder, the mismatch between scroll input and visual motion is a direct trigger for dizziness and nausea within seconds, often before they've found a way to stop scrolling.

contentSections.scenario: The parallax effect above is triggered purely by the user scrolling — it has no function beyond visual style, and the page's content and layout are completely unaffected if it's removed.
contentSections.question: Under WCAG 2.3.3 Animation from Interactions (AAA), what does this interface owe a user experiencing symptoms from it?

options.label: Nothing — 2.3.3 only applies to autoplaying video, not scroll-triggered effects
A way to disable the motion, because it's triggered by user interaction (scrolling) and isn't essential to the content or functionality
A warning label before the page loads

feedback.wrong: 2.3.3 is written broadly around interaction-triggered motion animation — scrolling, hovering, or any user input that sets something moving — not just video playback specifically.
feedback.disable: Right. 2.3.3 requires motion animation triggered by interaction to be disable-able unless the motion is essential to the functionality or the information being conveyed. Purely decorative parallax has no function beyond style, which puts it squarely inside what the criterion requires a way to turn off.
feedback.warning: A warning tells someone the harm is coming without preventing it — useful as an addition, never a substitute for an actual mechanism to disable the motion before it happens.

contentSections.concept: **2.3.3 draws a specific line: interaction-triggered motion has to be disable-able unless it's essential.** 'Essential' is a narrow, real category — a drag-and-drop reordering interaction needs the dragged element to visibly move, or the interaction doesn't make sense at all. Purely decorative motion — parallax, elements that slide or bounce in on scroll with no functional purpose — almost never clears that bar, and 'it looks polished' is not the same claim as 'the motion is essential to the content or function.'

contentSections.body: This is a genuinely physical barrier, not an aesthetic preference — vestibular symptoms from a mismatch between visual motion and the body's own sense of movement are a real, physiological response, not a matter of some users simply disliking animation. Reduced-motion isn't a stylistic accommodation the way a light/dark mode toggle is; treating it as equivalent to a cosmetic preference understates what's actually at stake for the person it's built for.
Interaction-triggered motion with no function beyond visual style has to be disable-able under 2.3.3 — 'essential' is a narrow bar that decorative parallax and slide-in effects almost never clear.

contentSections.title: The reduced-motion fix that breaks the loading spinner

contentSections.body: A developer implements `prefers-reduced-motion` support in one line: `@media (prefers-reduced-motion: reduce) { * { animation: none !important; } }`. It works — parallax and slide-in effects stop. It also removes the loading spinner's animation entirely, so anyone with reduced motion enabled now sees a static, motionless circle during a genuine loading state, with no way to tell whether the page is working or stuck.

contentSections.scenario: The universal `* { animation: none }` rule silences every animation on the page, decorative and functional alike, the moment reduced-motion is enabled.
contentSections.question: What's the actual mechanism behind the loading spinner breaking?

options.label: The selector is too broad — it treats every animation on the page as equally optional, when a loading spinner's motion is the only signal that a process is actually running, not decoration
prefers-reduced-motion isn't meant to be implemented this simply — it requires a JavaScript-based solution
Loading spinners should never animate for anyone, reduced-motion or not

feedback.jsonly: The media query itself is the right tool and works fine in pure CSS — the actual defect is scope, applying one blanket rule to every animation regardless of whether that specific animation is decorative or functional.
feedback.toobroad: Right. A universal selector treats a decorative slide-in and a functional loading indicator identically, when only one of them is actually optional. The fix needs to distinguish the two, not silence everything equally.
feedback.neveranimate: A loading spinner's motion is exactly the kind of essential, low-amplitude, non-parallax motion that reduced-motion preferences aren't meant to remove — the goal is removing motion that could trigger symptoms, not all visual feedback whatsoever.

contentSections.mechanism: **prefers-reduced-motion has to be scoped to decorative and large-amplitude motion specifically, not applied as a blanket 'turn off all animation' switch.** The correct fix keeps a genuinely essential status indicator working — often by swapping a large-amplitude spinner for a smaller, gentler pulsing dot or an opacity fade rather than removing feedback entirely — while disabling parallax, bounce-in, and other motion with no functional purpose. A user who enabled reduced motion specifically to stop feeling sick from scroll effects still needs to know whether a page is loading or frozen.

contentSections.body: The honest scoping test worth applying to any animation before deciding its fate under a reduced-motion rule: does removing this motion delete information the user needs (a loading state, a drag position, a progress indicator), or does it only remove visual flourish? The first category needs a gentler substitute, not a removal; the second can simply be turned off.

A blanket 'no animation' rule under reduced-motion silences functional feedback along with decoration — the fix distinguishes essential motion (which needs a gentler substitute) from decorative motion (which can simply stop).

title: Auto-play, carousels and things that move without asking
description: A hero carousel that advances every four seconds and a video that starts playing with sound the instant a page loads fail two different WCAG criteria for two different reasons — one is about motion, one is about audio, and they need two separate fixes.

learningObjectives.text: Apply WCAG 2.2.2 Pause, Stop, Hide to auto-advancing content
Apply WCAG 1.4.2 Audio Control to autoplaying audio
Distinguish a motion-based autoplay failure from an audio-based one

contentSections.title: The carousel that won't hold still

contentSections.body: A homepage hero banner cycles through five promotional slides automatically, four seconds each, on a continuous loop, with no visible pause button anywhere. For someone trying to read the second slide's text, it's gone before they finish the first sentence — and for someone sensitive to repeated motion, the loop simply never stops.

contentSections.scenario: The carousel auto-advances every 4 seconds, runs indefinitely, and sits alongside other page content (navigation, body text) rather than being the only thing on the page.
contentSections.question: Does this carousel need a pause/stop/hide mechanism under WCAG 2.2.2?

options.label: No — 2.2.2 only applies to video and audio, not image carousels
Yes — moving content that starts automatically, lasts more than 5 seconds, and is presented alongside other content needs a way to pause, stop, or hide it
Only if the carousel includes text on the images

feedback.no: 2.2.2 is written around moving, blinking, scrolling or auto-updating content generally — carousels, tickers, and auto-advancing image banners are squarely inside its scope, not just video or audio.
feedback.yes: Right. This carousel meets every condition 2.2.2 names: it starts automatically, it runs continuously (well past 5 seconds), and it's presented in parallel with other page content the user might be trying to read at the same time. All three together require a pause, stop, or hide control.
feedback.textonly: The presence of text isn't the trigger — the criterion is about the motion itself competing with a user's ability to read or focus on anything else on the page, regardless of what's printed on the moving slides.

contentSections.concept: **WCAG 2.2.2 Pause, Stop, Hide (A) applies to moving, blinking, scrolling or auto-updating content that starts automatically, lasts more than 5 seconds, and is presented in parallel with other content.** All three conditions together are what trigger the requirement — a carousel that auto-advances forever, next to a page someone is trying to read, is exactly the shape this criterion was written for. The fix is a visible, keyboard-reachable pause control, defaulting to paused-on-first-interaction is even better, not merely present somewhere hard to find.

contentSections.body: This connects directly to the module before this one's motion lesson: a carousel that auto-advances is a form of motion someone can't stop, and it's exactly the case 2.3.3's 'essential' exception doesn't cover — a carousel showing five different promotions has no functional need to advance on its own timer rather than waiting for a user's own click.
Auto-advance, runs past 5 seconds, sits alongside other content — a carousel meeting all three needs a real, visible pause control, and 'it's just images, not video' doesn't exempt it.

contentSections.title: The video that starts talking before you've clicked anything

contentSections.body: A product page embeds a promotional video that autoplays with sound the instant the page finishes loading, no click required. For someone using a screen reader, the video's audio now competes directly with their screen reader's own speech output — two voices talking over each other, with no obvious way to make either one stop.

contentSections.question: What does WCAG 1.4.2 Audio Control require for audio that plays automatically for more than 3 seconds?
contentSections.answer: A mechanism to pause or stop the audio, or to control its volume independently of the overall system volume, must be available. The 3-second threshold matters specifically: audio autoplaying for 3 seconds or less is exempt, on the reasoning that a very brief sound doesn't meaningfully compete with a screen reader for that long, but anything past that has to be controllable without the user needing to hunt for the system volume control.
contentSections.hint: This is a different criterion from the carousel's — think specifically about sound competing with a screen reader's own audio output, not visual motion.

contentSections.body: 1.4.2 and 2.2.2 are two separate criteria doing two separate jobs, worth keeping distinct in a finding even when one page fails both at once: 2.2.2 is about motion competing for visual attention and reading time, 1.4.2 is about sound competing directly with a screen reader's own speech. A muted autoplay video with visible motion still needs 2.2.2's pause control; the same video with sound also needs 1.4.2's audio control — fixing one doesn't fix the other, and a finding that only names one when both apply leaves real work undiscovered.

Motion and audio are two separate criteria with two separate fixes — a video that autoplays with sound needs both a way to stop the motion and a way to stop or control the audio, and naming only one leaves a real barrier unaddressed.

title: Flashing content and seizure risk: the actual thresholds
description: Seizure risk from flashing content has a real, specific, measurable threshold — and it's stricter for saturated red flashes than for any other color, which is exactly the detail a 'looks fast, probably fine' visual check misses.

learningObjectives.text: State the WCAG 2.3.1 flash-rate threshold precisely
Apply the general flash and red flash thresholds to a real animated element
Explain why red flashes get a stricter threshold than other colors

contentSections.title: The number that actually matters

contentSections.body: A 'Flash Sale' promotional banner does exactly what its name says — a bright yellow background rapidly alternates with white, meant to grab attention on a crowded page. Nobody on the design team asked how many times per second it was actually flashing before shipping it.

contentSections.scenario: WCAG 2.3.1 (Three Flashes or Below Threshold, A) sets a specific flash-rate limit for content that isn't otherwise restricted.
contentSections.question: How many flashes per second is the general threshold, above which content fails 2.3.1 outright (absent the below-threshold exceptions)?
contentSections.explanation: The threshold is more than 3 flashes in any one-second period. Content flashing 3 times per second or fewer passes outright. Above that rate, the content has to additionally pass the more detailed general flash and red flash area/contrast thresholds to be permitted at all — which most decorative promotional flashing effects were never tested against and typically fail. A 'Flash Sale' banner alternating rapidly enough to look urgent is very often flashing well above 3 times per second once actually measured, not just eyeballed.

contentSections.body: 'Below threshold' isn't just about the flash rate on its own — the general flash threshold also depends on the size of the flashing area (a flash covering a large portion of the viewport is riskier than a small icon) and the contrast between the two states. A banner that flashes at exactly 3 times a second but covers most of the screen at high contrast can still fail the fuller general flash threshold even while technically at the rate limit — the '3 flashes per second' number is the simplest part of a more detailed test, not the whole test by itself.

The flash-rate threshold is 3 per second — content above that rate has to clear the fuller general flash and red flash tests, which most decorative flashing effects were never designed or measured against.

contentSections.title: Why red gets its own, stricter rule

contentSections.body: A loading indicator uses a rapidly pulsing icon in saturated red, meant to signal urgency during a payment-processing wait. A user with photosensitive epilepsy reports it triggered a seizure aura, even though the same design team had separately confirmed the pulse rate was under the general 3-per-second threshold using a different, non-red test color during their own review.

contentSections.scenario: The pulsing icon passed a general flash-rate check using a placeholder gray color during design review, then shipped in saturated red — and still caused a real photosensitive reaction at a rate the team had already 'cleared.'
contentSections.question: What does this reveal about how the general flash threshold and the red flash threshold relate to each other?

options.label: Saturated red transitions have their own separate, stricter threshold — checking a design against the general flash rate using a different color doesn't clear the red flash threshold, which the actual shipped color is subject to independently
Nothing — if the general flash rate passes, color is irrelevant
The team's review method was fine; this was an unpredictable, unrelated medical event

feedback.irrelevant: Color is specifically not irrelevant here — the red flash threshold exists precisely because saturated red transitions carry elevated seizure risk independent of the general flash-rate number, which is exactly what this scenario demonstrates.
feedback.separate: Right. Testing a placeholder gray version and testing the actual shipped saturated-red version are two different tests with two different thresholds. Clearing one says nothing about the other — the red flash threshold is measured independently and is stricter specifically because saturated red transitions carry documented, elevated seizure risk beyond general luminance flashing.
feedback.unrelated: This is a directly foreseeable outcome of testing a placeholder color instead of the real, shipped one — 2.3.1's own structure (a general threshold and a separate red threshold) exists specifically because this exact substitution error is common and consequential.

contentSections.mechanism: **WCAG 2.3.1's general flash threshold and its red flash threshold are two independent tests, and a design has to clear both, tested against the actual colors that will ship — not a substitute or placeholder.** Saturated red transitions carry a documented, elevated photosensitive-seizure risk beyond ordinary luminance flashing, which is why the criterion doesn't treat 'flashing at an acceptable rate' as color-neutral. A review that tests a mockup in a neutral color and assumes the conclusion transfers to the shipped palette has tested the wrong thing.

contentSections.body: The practical implication for a review: flash-rate testing has to happen against the actual production colors and actual production speed, not a design-file approximation, and any element using saturated red specifically deserves its own explicit check rather than inheriting a pass from a same-speed, different-color element elsewhere on the page.
Red flash risk is measured separately from general flash risk — a design that passed at the right rate in the wrong color hasn't actually been tested, and shipping the real color needs its own check.

title: Audio, captions and transcripts done properly
description: A 'captions enabled' checkbox in a CMS confirms a captions track exists, not that it's accurate — auto-generated captions turning 'diabetes' into 'diet beat is' throughout a training video technically satisfy that checkbox and fail the person relying on them completely.

learningObjectives.text: Apply WCAG 1.2.2 Captions (Prerecorded) to caption accuracy, not just presence
Diagnose why unedited auto-generated captions are a real finding even when a captions track technically exists
Identify what a complete transcript includes beyond spoken dialogue

contentSections.title: A captions track that technically exists and doesn't actually work

contentSections.body: A healthcare company's mandatory training video has captions — the CMS shows a green checkmark next to 'Captions: enabled.' The captions are entirely auto-generated and never reviewed. Throughout the video, 'diabetes' is transcribed as 'diet beat is,' 'insulin' as 'in slid in,' and a key dosage instruction is garbled into something that doesn't parse as a sentence at all.

contentSections.scenario: The CMS's own compliance dashboard marks this video 'accessible: captions present.' A deaf employee relying entirely on the captions cannot determine the actual dosage instruction from what's displayed.
contentSections.question: Does a technically-present captions track satisfy WCAG 1.2.2 Captions (Prerecorded) if it's this inaccurate?

options.label: Yes — 1.2.2 only requires that captions exist, not that they're accurate
No — 1.2.2 requires captions that convey the actual spoken content; unreviewed auto-generated captions garbling key terms fail the criterion even though a captions track is technically present
It depends on whether the video has a separate written transcript available too

feedback.presence: A CMS checkbox tracking whether a captions file exists is a presence check, not a quality check — and 1.2.2's actual requirement is that captions provide equivalent access to the audio content, which garbled auto-generated text doesn't do regardless of whether a file technically exists.
feedback.accuracy: Right. A dashboard showing 'captions: enabled' is checking for a file's existence, which is a different question from whether that file actually conveys the audio. Captions this inaccurate, on content this consequential, fail the criterion's actual intent even while passing an automated presence check.
feedback.transcript: A separate transcript existing elsewhere doesn't fix captions that are wrong during video playback itself — someone watching the video relies on the captions in that moment, and a transcript filed elsewhere doesn't help them follow along in real time.

contentSections.concept: **A compliance dashboard checking 'does a captions file exist' is answering a different, easier question than WCAG 1.2.2 actually asks.** 1.2.2 requires captions for prerecorded audio content, and the unstated but real expectation behind that requirement is that the captions convey the content — unreviewed auto-generated captions on technical or medical terminology routinely garble exactly the words that matter most, which makes 'presence' a genuinely misleading proxy for 'compliance' on this specific criterion.

contentSections.body: This is a common, specific real-audit finding worth naming precisely, because 'the video has captions' will be the org's honest first answer and the actual finding needs to go one level deeper: request the caption file directly, play the video with captions on and audio off, and check whether the content is actually followable — particularly through any specialised vocabulary the auto-caption model is likely to mishear. A caption file that's never been reviewed by a human is a strong predictor of exactly this failure on any content with domain-specific terms.

'Captions enabled' in a CMS checks for a file's existence, not its accuracy — unreviewed auto-generated captions on technical content routinely fail the person relying on them while passing that checkbox.

contentSections.title: What a transcript owes beyond the dialogue

contentSections.body: A product-demo video's transcript is a clean, accurate word-for-word record of everything anyone says. At one point in the video, a presenter gasps audibly and the room laughs when a new feature works unexpectedly well — neither is in the transcript, which reads as a flat technical monologue with no indication anything notable happened at that moment.

contentSections.question: Does an accurate, complete transcript of everything that was said fully substitute for the video, if it omits non-speech audio like a gasp, laughter, or a meaningful pause?
contentSections.answer: Not fully. A complete transcript includes significant non-speech audio in bracketed descriptions — [gasps], [audience laughs], [long pause] — wherever it carries real meaning, not only the literal words spoken. A transcript that's accurate on dialogue but silent on everything else can miss the emotional or reactive context a hearing viewer picks up automatically, which matters most exactly in moments (surprise, humor, tension) where the non-speech audio is doing real communicative work.
contentSections.hint: Think about everything a hearing viewer perceives in that moment beyond the literal words — what does silence in the transcript at that point actually communicate, versus what a viewer with sound heard?

contentSections.body: The same principle extends to speaker identification in any multi-person recording — a transcript that doesn't mark who's speaking when multiple people talk leaves a reader unable to follow a conversation the way a listener naturally can from voice alone, and that gap grows worse, not better, in exactly the discussions (disagreement, interruption, a change of mind) where knowing who said what matters most.

A transcript that's word-perfect on dialogue and silent on everything else still loses real meaning — significant non-speech sound and speaker identification are both part of what makes a transcript a genuine equivalent, not an optional extra.

title: Visual noise and interfaces that are exhausting to parse
description: A dashboard where nothing individually fails a single WCAG criterion can still be genuinely exhausting to look at — competing colors, simultaneous motion, and a dozen equally-loud focal points add up to a real sensory cost no single-element check will ever catch.

learningObjectives.text: Evaluate an interface for cumulative visual load rather than single-element compliance
Distinguish genuine visual-noise reduction from changes that only look calmer
Name the honest limits of WCAG's coverage for cumulative sensory load

contentSections.title: Nothing here individually fails, and all of it together is exhausting

contentSections.body: A logistics dashboard shows fourteen status tiles, each a different saturated color, three of them with a subtle pulsing animation, a notification badge in the corner of nine of them, and a ticking countdown timer at the top of the page. Every individual element passes its own contrast check and its own animation isn't fast enough to trip the flash threshold. Using it for ten minutes leaves a genuinely fatigued, wrung-out feeling that no single element explains on its own.

contentSections.scenario: A redesign proposal for this dashboard suggests several changes.
contentSections.question: Which of these genuinely reduce the cumulative sensory load? Select all that apply.

items.label: Use color purposefully — one consistent color meaning 'needs attention,' rather than fourteen tiles each in a different saturated color with no shared meaning
Limit animation to at most one element at a time, reserved for something that genuinely needs attention right now
Show notification badges only for tiles that actually need action, not as a default decoration on every tile
Remove all color entirely and render every tile in identical grayscale 'to eliminate visual noise'
Make the whole dashboard auto-refresh every 2 seconds so information is always maximally current

explanation.one-color-per-meaning: Yes — color used consistently to mean one specific thing lets a viewer parse the dashboard at a glance; fourteen unrelated colors force re-evaluation of every tile individually since none of them carry a shared, learnable meaning.
explanation.reduce-simultaneous-motion: Yes — multiple independent moving elements compete for attention simultaneously; limiting motion to what's actually urgent right now removes competing signals rather than adding a rule about how fast any one of them moves.
explanation.badge-triage: Yes — a badge on every tile by default carries no information (everything is 'flagged,' so nothing is), while a badge that only appears when action is actually needed becomes a real, load-bearing signal again.
explanation.monochrome-everything: No — removing color entirely also removes color's genuine usefulness for meaning (an actual attention-needed state), trading one problem (too much undifferentiated color) for a different one (no differentiation at all).
explanation.auto-refresh-fast: No — a page visibly changing every 2 seconds is itself a form of constant motion and a fresh demand on attention every time something updates, which increases cumulative load rather than reducing it, even though the underlying goal (current information) is reasonable.

contentSections.synthesis: Three of these changes reduce load by making color, motion and badges carry real, consistent meaning instead of competing decoration. The other two chase a different goal — visual minimalism, maximal freshness — and in doing so remove or add load in a different form. The actual target isn't 'less of everything' or 'more of everything,' it's fewer things demanding attention at once, and each one meaning something specific when it does.

contentSections.body: The honest limit worth naming directly, echoing the earlier module's pattern: WCAG has no single criterion measuring cumulative visual density or competing simultaneous signals the way it has a specific number for flash rate or a specific ratio for contrast. A page can pass every individual contrast check, every individual animation-timing check, and every individual color-use check, and still be genuinely exhausting to use — which means this is exactly the kind of finding that belongs in a good audit as an evaluative judgment, not something to leave out because no clean citation covers the whole pattern at once.
A page where every individual element passes its own check can still be exhausting as a whole — cumulative visual load has no single WCAG number, and a good audit names it anyway.

contentSections.title: What looks calmer and isn't

contentSections.body: A follow-up redesign of the same dashboard removes every solid background color, replacing all fourteen tiles with thin white cards on a white page, distinguished only by faint 1px gray borders. The design team calls it 'decluttered.'

contentSections.code: Redesign notes: 'Removed all tile background colors. All 14 tiles are now white cards with a 1px #e5e5e5 border, distinguished only by their text labels. Feels much calmer.'
contentSections.question: What's the actual problem with this specific fix?

options.label: It reduces visual noise correctly and has no real downside

It removes color's genuine usefulness (a fast, glanceable way to spot which tile needs attention) and replaces it with nothing — now every tile requires reading its text label individually to tell them apart, which is a different, arguably worse cognitive cost than the original noise
White backgrounds always fail WCAG contrast requirements

feedback.correct: This looks calmer at a glance, which is exactly the trap — the actual cognitive task ('which of these fourteen tiles needs my attention right now') got harder, not easier, once color stopped doing any of that work.
feedback.newload: Right. This is the same shape of mistake as the earlier module's 'fewer clicks isn't the same as less cognitive load' pattern — 'calmer-looking' isn't the same as 'genuinely lower load.' Removing color's actual function (fast differentiation) without replacing it with anything shifts the cost onto reading every label individually, which is slower and more effortful than a well-used color system would have been.
feedback.contrast: Contrast ratio isn't the mechanism here — a 1px light gray border against white could genuinely fail contrast on its own, but that's a separate, narrower finding from the actual problem: color's differentiating function was removed and never replaced.

contentSections.flawExplanation: This redesign optimises for a look — calm, decluttered, minimal — the same way the cognitive-load module's 'merge five screens into one' example optimised for click count while making the actual underlying task harder. The right fix keeps color's real job (fast differentiation of what needs attention) while making it purposeful rather than decorative — one meaningful color for 'needs action,' neutral tones for everything else — not stripping color out entirely and calling the absence of noise the same thing as the presence of clarity.

contentSections.body: A design that looks calmer isn't automatically lower-load — removing color's real differentiating function without replacing it just moves the cost onto reading every label individually.

title: Practice — Assess Eight Interfaces for Sensory Barriers
description: Eight drills across the module's skills. No new concepts: this is where telling a real motion, flash or audio barrier from a merely decorative choice stops being something you've read about.

learningObjectives.text: Apply motion, flash-threshold, audio and caption judgement to unfamiliar interfaces at speed
Distinguish a genuine sensory-load reduction from a change that only looks calmer

contentSections.title: Eight drills

contentSections.body: Nothing new here. Eight drills across the module's skills, ordered from where the lessons ended to one step past it. Do them in one sitting if that works, or spread across several — the set doesn't expire and nothing is timed.
If a drill needed a hint, that's the thing to watch for in the checkpoint — not a reason to redo the set.

title: Lab — Run a Sensory-Load Review of a Media-Heavy Page
description: Pick a real page with video, animation or a dense layout and walk it once for motion, once for audio, once for flash risk, and once for cumulative visual load — four different lenses on the same page, because each one catches something the others miss.

learningObjectives.text: Test a real page against motion, autoplay, flash-threshold and captioning criteria
Evaluate cumulative visual load as a distinct finding from any single-element check
Write specific, implementable sensory-load reductions

contentSections.title: The lab

contentSections.body: Pick a real, media-heavy page you can access today — a news homepage, a product page with video, a marketing landing page with animation. This lab produces a sensory-load review across motion, autoplay, flash, captions and visual density, not a redesign.

contentSections.title: Sensory-load review of a media-heavy page
contentSections.brief: Choose a real page with at least one of: autoplaying media, animation, or a visually dense layout. Review it once for motion (interaction-triggered and auto-advancing), once for audio (autoplay and captions), and once for cumulative visual load — even where no single element fails a specific criterion.
contentSections.deliverable: A review covering motion, autoplay, flash thresholds, captions and visual density, with a specific reduction proposed for each finding.

stages.title: Motion and autoplay pass
stages.instructions: Identify every animated or auto-advancing element (parallax, carousels, auto-play video). For each, check: is it disable-able (2.3.3)? Does it meet the auto-advance/pause conditions of 2.2.2? If a prefers-reduced-motion preference is respected, check it doesn't also silence essential motion (loading states, progress indicators).
stages.checkpoint: Every moving element is logged with its trigger, duration, and whether a pause/disable mechanism exists.

stages.title: Audio, captions and flash pass
stages.instructions: For any autoplaying audio, check for a stop/mute mechanism independent of system volume (1.4.2). For any video, check captions with audio off — are they accurate, not just present? Check any rapidly-flashing element against the 3-per-second threshold, with particular attention to saturated red elements.
stages.checkpoint: Every audio/video element has a captions-accuracy note, and any flashing element has an estimated flash rate and color noted.

stages.title: Cumulative visual load and reductions, with self-check
stages.instructions: Step back from individual elements and assess the page as a whole: how many things are competing for attention at once (color, motion, badges)? Write this as an evaluative finding even with no single citation covering it. For every finding across all three passes, write a specific, implementable reduction. Then run the self-check below.
stages.checkpoint: Every finding has a named location, a specific cost, and a specific reduction — including at least one cumulative-load finding logged without a forced citation.

rubric.criterion: Motion, audio and flash are each checked against their own specific criterion
rubric.meets: A reader can see which WCAG criterion (or threshold) each motion, audio and flash finding is tested against, and that they weren't conflated.

rubric.criterion: Caption accuracy is verified, not just caption presence
rubric.meets: At least one caption finding states whether the captions were actually reviewed with audio off, not just confirmed to exist.

rubric.criterion: Cumulative visual load is assessed as its own finding
rubric.meets: The review includes at least one evaluative finding about the page as a whole, not only single-element checks.

rubric.criterion: Every reduction is specific and implementable
rubric.meets: A developer reading only the reduction would know exactly what to change.

rubric.criterion: The review reflects a real energy budget
rubric.meets: The stages were completed as separate sittings if needed — nothing about the review required one unbroken 50-minute block.

contentSections.body: A page reviewed only element by element can pass every individual check and still be a real sensory cost as a whole — this lab is the difference between confirming each piece is fine and confirming the page actually is.

title: Checkpoint — Motion, Sound and Sensory Load
description: Ten questions: four from this module, four from the module before it in this course, and two from the module two back in this course. Ungraded, untimed, and getting one wrong just means it comes back later.

learningObjectives.text: Retrieve this module's motion, sound and sensory load distinctions alongside the previous module's content and language distinctions and the cognitive load distinctions two modules back, without looking them up

contentSections.title: Let's see what stuck
Checkpoint — Motion, Sound and Sensory Load

questions.from: This module — Motion, Sound and Sensory Load
questions.prompt: A purely decorative parallax scroll effect, triggered by scrolling, has no function beyond visual style. What does WCAG 2.3.3 require?

options.label: Nothing — 2.3.3 only covers autoplaying video
A way to disable it, since it's interaction-triggered motion with no essential function
A warning label is sufficient on its own

questions.explanation: 2.3.3 requires interaction-triggered motion animation to be disable-able unless it's essential to the content or function — purely decorative parallax almost never clears that bar.

questions.from: This module — Motion, Sound and Sensory Load
questions.prompt: A hero carousel auto-advances every 4 seconds, runs indefinitely, alongside other page content, with no pause button. What does this fail?

options.label: Nothing — carousels aren't covered by WCAG
WCAG 2.2.2 Pause, Stop, Hide — content that auto-starts, exceeds 5 seconds, and runs alongside other content needs a pause/stop/hide mechanism
Only a problem if the carousel includes video, not images

questions.explanation: All three conditions (auto-start, past 5 seconds, parallel with other content) together trigger 2.2.2's requirement for a visible, reachable pause control.

questions.from: This module — Motion, Sound and Sensory Load
questions.prompt: A design passed a flash-rate check using a placeholder gray color, then shipped in saturated red at the same rate. Why might it still fail?

options.label: Saturated red transitions have their own, stricter threshold, tested independently of the general flash-rate check
It can't fail — passing the general rate means any color is safe
Red only matters if the flash rate exceeds 10 per second

questions.explanation: The red flash threshold is a separate, stricter test from the general flash threshold — clearing one using a different color doesn't clear the other for the actual shipped color.

questions.from: This module — Motion, Sound and Sensory Load
questions.prompt: A CMS shows 'Captions: enabled' for a training video whose auto-generated captions garble key technical terms throughout. Does this satisfy WCAG 1.2.2?

options.label: Yes — 1.2.2 only requires that a captions file exist
No — captions this inaccurate fail to convey the actual content, even though a captions track is technically present
Yes, as long as a separate written transcript exists somewhere else

questions.explanation: A presence check ('does a file exist') is a different, easier question than whether the captions actually convey the audio content — unreviewed auto-generated captions on technical terms routinely fail the second question.

questions.from: Previous module — Content, Language and Reading
questions.prompt: A plain-language rewrite of a denial letter is shorter and friendlier but no longer states the actual reason for the denial. What's the right read?

options.label: It's an improvement — shorter and friendlier is always more accessible
It's not genuine plain language — it deleted the information the reader needs to act, trading one failure for another
It's fine as long as it passes a readability score

questions.explanation: Plain language means stating necessary complexity clearly, not deleting it — a rewrite missing the actual reason has a different failure than the dense original, not a fix for it.

questions.from: Previous module — Content, Language and Reading
questions.prompt: Ten 'Read more' links, each inside a paragraph naming a different headline, might pass WCAG 2.4.4. Why can this still be a real problem?

options.label: It isn't a problem once 2.4.4 passes
A link-list view strips away the surrounding paragraph, so ten identical link texts defeat that navigation method entirely, even where in-context purpose is technically determinable
'Read more' always fails 2.4.4 regardless of context

questions.explanation: 2.4.9 exists specifically because link-list navigation removes all surrounding context — passing 2.4.4 doesn't mean link-list navigation still works.

questions.from: Previous module — Content, Language and Reading
questions.prompt: An error message reads 'Invalid password,' correctly placed with focus moved to it. Why is this still an incomplete finding?

options.label: Placement and focus are the only requirements
It identifies that something is wrong but suggests no fix — the content, not just the position, has to name the rule and the fix
It needs a different color

questions.explanation: 3.3.1 and 3.3.3 both concern content — a well-placed message naming no specific rule still fails to suggest an actual fix.

questions.from: Two modules back — Cognitive Accessibility
questions.prompt: How does the lesson say cognitive barriers should be treated when no single WCAG criterion covers them?

options.label: They are left out because they cannot be tested pass or fail
They are named as findings on their own evaluative merits
They are reported if the client asks about them directly

questions.explanation: COGA guidance is largely advisory, and a lot of it does not fit a pass or fail criterion. That does not make it less real, so the report names the barrier anyway.

questions.from: Two modules back — Cognitive Accessibility
questions.prompt: A timed form session has no warning before it logs the user out. Which two fixes does the lesson name, and why both?

options.label: A warning with an extend option, plus autosave for missed ones
A longer timeout for all users, plus a larger logout button
A warning alone, since autosave is a security risk for forms

questions.explanation: The two fixes solve different halves of the problem. A form as effortful as a long application form warrants both, not either.

questions.from: Previous module — Content, Language and Reading
questions.prompt: An icon-only button shows a download arrow and downloads a spec sheet PDF. What should its text alternative carry?

options.label: A description of the icon, such as a grey downward arrow
The action it performs, such as Download spec sheet (PDF)
An empty alt value, because the arrow is plain decoration

questions.explanation: A functional image is a control, so its text alternative names what activating it does. An empty alt would leave the button with no accessible name, and a description of the arrow's shape does not say what pressing it does.

contentSections.body: None of these need to be perfect. What matters is which ones needed a guess — that's what the next checkpoint will bring back.

title: Counting the interactions a task actually requires
description: Booking a follow-up appointment on a phone while tired and interrupted turns out to take fourteen taps when six would genuinely do — the difference between those two numbers is the entire finding, and nobody sees it until they actually count.

learningObjectives.text: Build an interaction inventory for a real task, counting every tap, click and decision
Classify each interaction as essential to the task or avoidable overhead
Distinguish an essential decision from a step that exists only because nobody removed it

contentSections.title: Fourteen taps for a task that needs six

contentSections.body: Booking a follow-up cardiology appointment, done lying down with the phone propped against a pillow because sitting upright long enough to finish it isn't an option today: open the app, log in, enter a 2FA code read off a different device, tap 'Appointments,' tap 'Book new,' select a department from a list where this clinic only has one department, select the one provider on the list, select a date, select a time, fill six form fields (four of which duplicate the profile already on file), tap 'Continue,' tap 'Confirm' on a summary screen, tap 'Confirm' again on a popup asking to confirm the confirmation, then open a separate confirmation email and tap a link inside it to 'finalise' the booking.

contentSections.scenario: The flow described above, counted as every distinct tap or required decision from opening the app to a booking that's actually confirmed.
contentSections.question: How many separate taps or decisions does this specific flow require?
contentSections.explanation: Fourteen. Of those, a genuinely defensible minimum for this task is closer to six: log in, pick a date, pick a time, fill in the (non-duplicate) reason for the visit, confirm once. The other eight — a department selector with one option, four fields that already exist on the profile, a second confirm on top of the first, and an external email click required to 'finalise' something already confirmed in-app — exist for reasons that have nothing to do with what the task actually requires. Counted honestly, this flow is more than double the length the task itself demands.

contentSections.body: This is the whole method, and it's almost insultingly simple to describe: list every tap, click, or decision a real task requires, in order, without skipping the tedious ones. Most teams never do this, because a flow feels fine when you're the person who built it and already know exactly where everything is. The list itself is the finding — a stakeholder who won't accept 'this feels like a lot of steps' will often accept 'here are the fourteen numbered steps, and here's the six-step version that loses no real functionality.'

The classification that matters is essential versus avoidable, not big versus small. A single-option department selector is a small, one-tap step and pure overhead — nothing is actually being chosen. Picking a specific appointment time is also one tap and completely essential — real information the system doesn't have any other way to get. Counting steps without classifying them treats these as equivalent, which misses the point entirely; a six-step essential flow and a six-step flow with two pieces of overhead removed from a longer one are both 'six steps,' and only one of them is actually as short as it can get.
Count every tap without skipping the boring ones, then classify each as essential or avoidable — the finding isn't the total number, it's the gap between the total and the honestly-necessary minimum.

contentSections.title: The method, worked twice

contentSections.body: The same counting method, applied to a second task, to see the pattern generalise rather than treating the appointment example as a one-off.

contentSections.problem: Build an interaction inventory for renewing a repeat prescription in a pharmacy app, and classify each step.

steps.label: List every step in order
steps.work: Open app → log in → tap 'Prescriptions' → tap 'Repeat prescriptions' → select the medication from a list of one → tap 'Request renewal' → answer a 'has anything changed?' screening question → tap 'Choose pharmacy' → select from a list of one saved pharmacy → tap 'Confirm request' → tap 'Confirm' again on a second summary screen.
steps.why: Writing every step down, including the ones that feel too small to mention, is what makes the list honest — skipping 'obviously fine' steps is exactly how overhead gets missed.

steps.label: Mark each step essential or avoidable
steps.work: Essential: log in (security), the screening question (a real clinical safety check), the final confirm. Avoidable: selecting a medication from a list of exactly one option, selecting a pharmacy from a list of exactly one option, and a second confirm screen repeating the first.
steps.why: A single-option list is never a real decision — the system already has enough information to skip straight past it, and asking anyway adds a tap that produces no new information.

steps.label: Total the honest minimum
steps.work: 10 steps as built; a defensible minimum removes the two single-option selectors and the duplicate confirm, landing at 7 — still safe, still clinically sound, genuinely shorter.
steps.why: The screening question and the confirmation stay, because they're doing real work (safety, intent) — the cut only removes steps that ask for information the system already has.

faded.problem: A second task: cancelling a subscription. Steps as built: open app → log in → tap 'Account' → tap 'Subscription' → tap 'Manage' → tap 'Cancel subscription' → answer a mandatory 'why are you leaving?' dropdown → view a full-screen retention offer with no visible skip button until scrolling down → tap 'No thanks' → confirm cancellation → receive a confirmation email.

blanks.prompt: Which single step here is most clearly avoidable, not because it's small, but because it exists specifically to slow the user down rather than to gather real information? (name it in a few words)
blanks.answer: the full-screen retention offer with no visible skip button
accept: the hidden skip button on the retention offer
blanks.why: A mandatory step designed to be found and dismissed, rather than to collect information the system needs, is a different category from ordinary overhead — it's overhead added on purpose, which the next lesson in this module names directly.

blanks.prompt: Is the 'why are you leaving?' dropdown essential or avoidable, given it's mandatory to proceed?
accept: avoidable, since it's optional information forced to be mandatory
blanks.why: Feedback about why someone is leaving can be genuinely useful to a business, but making it mandatory to complete a task the user has already decided on adds a forced step that isn't required to actually perform the cancellation itself — it should be optional, not blocking.

blanks.prompt: What's the honest minimum step count for this task, cutting only the retention offer's forced friction and making the survey optional? (a number)
blanks.why: Open, log in, navigate to subscription (3 taps of navigation), cancel, confirm, done — roughly 7 steps is a genuinely defensible minimum; the built version pads that with a screen specifically engineered to cost the user extra time and attention.

contentSections.procedure: **The inventory method is the same regardless of the task: list every step honestly, classify each as essential (the system needs this information) or avoidable (a single-option list, a duplicate confirmation, or friction added on purpose), and total the honest minimum.** The gap between the built version and the honest minimum is the finding — and as the cancellation example starts to show, some of that gap isn't accidental at all, which is exactly what the rest of this module gets into.

contentSections.body: The inventory method works the same on any task: list it honestly, classify each step, total the minimum — and watch for the steps that aren't accidental overhead but friction someone added on purpose.

title: Session timeouts and the user who steps away
description: A warn-and-extend session timeout satisfies WCAG 2.2.1 cleanly — and still isn't enough for an interruption whose length nobody, including the person having it, can predict in advance.

learningObjectives.text: Evaluate whether a session-timeout mitigation actually protects an unpredictable-duration interruption
Distinguish a WCAG-compliant timeout mechanism from one that's actually sufficient for this specific user
Explain why autosave functions as close to essential for energy-limited users even where it isn't formally required

contentSections.title: Twenty minutes wasn't the plan

contentSections.body: Someone is halfway through a long disability-benefits application, typing detailed answers about their own medical history, when their heart rate spikes and their vision starts greying out — the start of a presyncope episode. There's no negotiating with this: they have to lie down immediately, and they have no way to know in advance whether that's going to take five minutes or forty.

contentSections.scenario: Three versions of this same form. Version A: a fixed 15-minute timeout with no warning at all. Version B: a warning at minute 13 offering to extend the session by 10x the default (150 minutes) — comfortably clearing WCAG 2.2.1. Version C: the same warning and extend option as B, plus autosave writing the form's contents to a draft every time a field changes.
contentSections.question: Which version actually protects this specific person's forty minutes of typed answers?

options.label: Version B — a 10x extension is what 2.2.1 requires, so it's sufficient

Version C — autosave is the only mechanism here that protects the data regardless of how long the interruption actually turns out to last, or whether the person is even at their screen to see or act on a warning
All three are equally fine, since 2.2.1 doesn't require autosave

feedback.b: Version B meets WCAG 2.2.1's letter, and it still assumes the person is present to see and act on a warning dialog — someone who just had to lie down mid-episode isn't at their screen to click 'extend,' regardless of how generous the extension multiplier is.
feedback.c: Right. Autosave is the only one of the three that doesn't depend on the person being present, attentive, or able to predict how long they'll be gone. A presyncope episode doesn't pause for a warning dialog, and its length isn't knowable in advance — the only mechanism that survives that unpredictability is one that doesn't require anyone to act during the interruption at all.
feedback.equal: 2.2.1 not requiring autosave settles what's formally mandated, not what actually protects this specific person — Version B can be fully compliant and still lose everything the moment the warning goes unanswered, which is exactly what's at risk here.

contentSections.concept: **A warn-and-extend mechanism protects a predictable, bounded interruption — someone who steps away knowing roughly how long they'll be gone, and who's able to act on a warning when they return or before they leave.** It does not protect an interruption whose length and the person's ability to respond are both unknown in the moment it starts, which is exactly what a dysautonomia episode, a migraine aura, or a sudden fatigue crash actually is. This isn't a claim that 2.2.1 is wrong or insufficiently strict — it's a claim that meeting 2.2.1 and actually protecting this specific, real interruption are two different outcomes, and a finding that only checks the first will miss the second completely.

contentSections.body: This directly extends the earlier module's honest finding about 2.2.1: a warning-plus-extend mechanism can be fully, correctly compliant and someone can still lose real work, because 2.2.1 doesn't require autosave and autosave is the only thing that would have protected this specific person. That module named it as a best-practice gap worth recommending on top of already-compliant behaviour. This module adds the sharper version of that same point: for a user whose interruptions are physically involuntary and unpredictable in length, that 'best practice' functions much closer to essential than optional, even though it isn't formally required by the letter of any WCAG criterion.

A warn-and-extend timeout protects someone who can predict and act on an interruption — it does nothing for someone whose interruption is involuntary and unpredictable in length, which is exactly when autosave stops being optional in practice.

contentSections.title: Why the multiplier doesn't rescue the mechanism

contentSections.body: A well-meaning engineer, reading the previous pod, proposes a fix: make the extension even more generous — instead of 10x the default (150 minutes on a 15-minute base), extend it to 24 hours whenever the warning is triggered. Problem solved?

contentSections.scenario: The extended session length is now generous enough to cover almost any realistic interruption — but the mechanism still requires the user to see the warning dialog and click 'extend' before the original, unextended timer runs out.
contentSections.question: Does making the extension longer actually fix the gap from the first pod?

options.label: Yes — a long enough extension window solves the problem for any interruption, regardless of length

No — the extension only helps once it's been triggered, and triggering it still requires the person to be present and responsive at the moment the warning appears, which is exactly what's not guaranteed during an involuntary episode
Yes, as long as the warning appears early enough in the session

feedback.yes: The extension length only matters after it's successfully triggered — and the actual gap is upstream of that, at the moment the warning appears and needs a response nobody can guarantee is coming.
feedback.no: Right. However generous the extension is, the mechanism still depends on the person seeing a dialog and clicking something at a moment they may already be mid-episode, away from the screen, or physically unable to interact with anything. A bigger number doesn't change what the mechanism requires of the user in that moment — it only changes what happens after that requirement is met.
feedback.early: An earlier warning gives slightly more lead time before the original timer expires, but doesn't change the core dependency: the person still has to be present and able to respond to it, at a moment whose timing they don't control.

contentSections.mechanism: **The gap isn't the size of the extension, it's the dependency on the user being present and responsive at all.** Any mechanism requiring an in-the-moment action — however generous the resulting grace period — fails for an interruption that removes the person's ability to act at exactly the moment the mechanism needs them to. Autosave sidesteps the dependency entirely: it doesn't ask anything of the person during the interruption, which is the actual property this specific situation requires, not a longer number.

contentSections.body: This is worth stating plainly in a finding, because 'just extend it further' is the natural first response and it doesn't reach the actual mechanism: the fix isn't a bigger timeout number, it's a mechanism that requires nothing from the user during the interruption at all. Autosave-to-draft, saved automatically and silently as the person types, is the shape of fix that actually matches this specific, real failure mode.

A longer extension window doesn't fix a mechanism that still depends on the user being present to trigger it — the actual fix removes that dependency entirely, which is what autosave does and a bigger timer number doesn't.

title: Work the interface makes you redo
description: Losing forty minutes of typed answers to a session timeout isn't just forty minutes lost — for someone on a fixed daily energy budget, it can mean the task doesn't get finished this week at all, because there may not be a second attempt in them today.

learningObjectives.text: Evaluate technical mitigations against whether they actually prevent redone work, not just reduce its likelihood
Explain why redone work costs more than its face-value time for someone on a limited energy budget
Apply graceful, incremental saving as the concrete fix for a specific redo-cost finding

contentSections.title: Forty minutes is not the actual cost

contentSections.body: The same benefits application from the previous lesson, this time from a different angle: the person doesn't get interrupted mid-episode, they simply take a genuinely reasonable amount of time thinking through how to phrase each answer about their own medical history, checking a specialist's letter for an exact date. Forty minutes in, with no autosave, the fixed session timer silently expires. Submitting throws an authentication error. Every answer is gone.

contentSections.scenario: A team reviewing this failure proposes several fixes.
contentSections.question: Which of these actually prevent work from being lost, rather than just making loss less likely?

items.label: Autosave the form's contents to a draft continuously as the user types, independent of the session timer
In a multi-page form, save each page's answers to the server the moment 'Next' is tapped, so a later failure only costs the current page, not every prior one
Extend the session timeout from 15 minutes to 45 minutes
Add a warning dialog at 13 minutes with no autosave behind it

explanation.autosave-draft: Yes — this is the only option that protects the actual content regardless of session length, interruption timing, or whether anyone sees or responds to a warning. It removes the possibility of loss rather than shrinking its likelihood.
explanation.per-page-save: Yes — even without full autosave, committing each completed page's answers before moving on means a later failure costs, at most, the current unsaved page — a genuinely smaller, bounded loss instead of an all-or-nothing one.
explanation.longer-timeout: No — this reduces how often the failure happens for someone who finishes within 45 minutes, and does nothing for anyone who takes longer, or who's interrupted regardless of the limit's length. It shrinks the odds without removing the actual risk.
explanation.warning-only: No — a warning with nothing behind it still loses everything the instant it's missed, whether from being away from the screen, an involuntary interruption, or simply not noticing a small dialog while concentrating on a hard question.

contentSections.synthesis: Two of these genuinely prevent loss because they save real data independent of the timer and independent of whether the user is present and responsive. The other two only make loss statistically less frequent, which is a different and much weaker property — a 45-minute limit still eventually gets hit by someone slower or more interrupted than the new number assumes, and a warning nobody can guarantee they'll see doesn't protect anyone who doesn't.

contentSections.body: The cost of redone work is not the minutes it takes to retype what was lost — for someone with a fixed, non-renewable daily budget of physical and cognitive effort, the actual cost is often that the task doesn't get finished today, or this week, at all. Retyping forty minutes of careful answers about your own medical history isn't a forty-minute inconvenience layered on top of the first attempt; it can be a second, separate expenditure the person genuinely doesn't have available, which is the difference between 'this was annoying' and 'I still haven't been able to apply for this benefit.'

This is worth stating in exactly those terms in a finding, because it's the argument that actually lands with a team that's used to thinking about lost work in minutes, not in whether the task gets completed at all: 'reduces the chance of data loss' and 'protects the user's ability to complete this task within their available capacity' are different claims, and only the second one is the actual requirement for someone whose capacity on a given day is a hard limit, not a preference.

The real cost of redone work isn't the retyping time — it's that a second attempt may not exist in someone's energy budget today at all, which is a different and much larger claim than 'this reduces how often data gets lost.'

contentSections.title: Saving in pieces instead of all at once

contentSections.body: A five-page medical intake form saves nothing until the very last page is submitted. A crash, a closed tab, or a session timeout on page 4 costs all four completed pages equally — the person who filled out page 1 correctly loses it exactly as completely as the half-finished page 4.

contentSections.question: Put these in the order a form should actually be engineered to bound the cost of a failure, from the most protective and simplest to add, to the most complete.
steps: Save each page's answers to the server the moment the user moves to the next page, so a failure at page 4 can never cost pages 1 through 3
Save within a page as individual fields are completed (not only on page transition), so a failure mid-page costs only the last few unsaved fields, not the whole page
On any crash, timeout, or return visit, restore the form exactly where the person left off, with everything already entered still visible
Give a visible, honest 'last saved' indicator so the person doesn't have to wonder whether their current answer is actually protected
contentSections.explanation: Per-page saving is the simplest change with the largest single improvement — it turns an all-or-nothing five-page loss into, at worst, a one-page loss. Per-field saving inside a page closes the remaining gap, bounding the cost even further. Restoring exactly where someone left off is what actually makes the saved data useful — data saved on a server that isn't offered back to the user on return doesn't save them any retyping. And a visible save indicator matters because someone deciding whether it's safe to stop and rest right now needs to know their answers are actually protected before making that call, not find out after the fact.
