contentSections.body: None of this requires exotic engineering — it's the same state-management principle from the earlier module's finding about clearing only the failed field instead of the whole form, applied at the scale of a whole multi-page flow instead of a single field. State held independently per page (or per field) survives a later failure by construction, the same way independently-validated fields survive a sibling field's error.
Saving in pieces — per page, then per field — bounds what a failure can cost to the smallest unit of real work, the same state-independence principle from a single field applied to an entire flow.

title: One-handed and small-screen use
description: A settings toggle that needs a long-press-then-drag gesture assumes two functioning hands and a flat surface — for someone holding a phone above their face with their other arm hooked up to an IV line, that assumption is the whole barrier.

learningObjectives.text: Evaluate an interaction for whether it's genuinely completable one-handed
Diagnose why thumb-reach zones change completely when a phone is held overhead rather than at a desk
Identify interactions that silently assume a seated posture and a free second hand

contentSections.title: The gesture that needs two hands to perform one-handed

contentSections.body: A grocery app lets users reorder items in a saved list, but only via long-press-then-drag: hold a finger on an item for a second, then drag it up or down while still holding. Doing this one-handed, on a phone held in the same hand doing the touching, means the phone itself has to stay perfectly still mid-gesture with no second hand free to steady it — for someone whose other arm is occupied (an IV line, a heating pad, a mobility aid), that's not a minor inconvenience, it's the point where the task stops being possible at all.

contentSections.scenario: Two versions of the same reorder feature. Version A: long-press-then-drag, requiring sustained contact and phone stability throughout. Version B: a visible 'Move up' / 'Move down' button pair next to each item, each a single, independent tap.
contentSections.question: Which version is genuinely completable with one hand holding an unsteadied phone?

options.label: Version A — drag gestures work fine on any touchscreen
Version B — a single discrete tap doesn't require the phone to stay perfectly still through a sustained gesture, and doesn't need a second hand to brace it
Both are equally usable one-handed — it depends only on thumb length

feedback.a: A drag gesture works fine on a stable surface with two hands available — one holding the device steady, one performing the gesture. It's a specific, narrower assumption than 'any touchscreen,' and it's exactly the assumption that breaks for someone with only one hand free.
feedback.b: Right. A single, discrete tap doesn't require the device to stay still through a sustained motion, and doesn't need a second hand to hold anything steady while the gesture happens — it's completable by the same thumb that's already holding the phone.
feedback.both: Thumb length affects reach, which matters separately — but the core difference here is about sustained-contact-plus-stability versus a single discrete tap, which is a mechanical difference independent of anyone's specific thumb length.

contentSections.concept: **A gesture that needs the device held steady through a sustained motion silently assumes a second hand, or a flat surface, is available.** Long-press-and-drag, pinch-to-zoom, and multi-finger gestures all carry this same hidden assumption. A single discrete tap on a clearly labelled 'move up' or 'move down' control performs the identical function with none of it — same outcome, no assumption about a stable surface or a free hand baked into the interaction itself.

contentSections.body: This connects to keyboard operability from the assistive-tech phase in an unexpected way: an interface with a genuine single-tap alternative to a complex gesture is very often, for entirely separate structural reasons, easier to also make keyboard-operable, since discrete, addressable controls translate cleanly to discrete key presses in a way a continuous drag gesture never fully does. Building the one-handed-friendly version and the keyboard-accessible version often turns out to be close to the same piece of work, not two separate accommodations competing for engineering time.

A sustained gesture like drag-to-reorder quietly assumes a second free hand or a stable surface — a single discrete tap achieves the same result without either assumption, and often ends up more keyboard-accessible too.

contentSections.title: Where the buttons are when you're lying on your side

contentSections.body: A medication-tracking app's most important action — 'Log dose taken' — sits at the very top of a tall scrolling screen, above a large decorative header image. On a desk, reaching the top of the screen with a thumb is trivial. Held overhead while lying on your back, or held out to the side while lying on your side, the top of a large phone screen is often the single hardest place on the entire display to reach with the thumb of the hand holding it.

contentSections.code:
Screen layout, top to bottom:
1. Decorative hero image (180px)
2. App logo and greeting text
3. "Log dose taken" primary button
4. Today's dose history
5. Secondary navigation
contentSections.question: What's the actual defect in this layout, specifically for one-handed, lying-down use?

options.label: The primary, most frequent action sits in the hardest-to-reach zone of the screen (the top) for a thumb operating one-handed, especially while lying down and holding the phone overhead or to the side, while a purely decorative image occupies prime, easy-to-reach space lower on the layout
Nothing — button placement doesn't matter as long as the button itself is large enough to tap accurately
The button should be a different color to stand out more

feedback.sizeonly: Target size (covered in the assistive-tech phase) matters for tapping accuracy once a thumb reaches the button — it says nothing about whether the thumb can comfortably get there in the first place, which is a separate, layout-level problem.
feedback.reach: Right. This is a reachability failure, not a size or contrast failure — the most frequent, most important action is placed exactly where a one-handed thumb, especially in a lying-down posture, has to stretch furthest to reach it, while a purely decorative image sits in genuinely easy reach doing nothing useful with that prime real estate.
feedback.color: Color would help the button stand out visually, which is a different problem from whether a thumb can physically reach it without repositioning the whole hand or using a second hand to help.

contentSections.flawExplanation: Standard thumb-reach research (built for seated, upright, desk-free phone use) already treats the bottom third of a large phone screen as the easiest zone and the top as the hardest — and that gap gets meaningfully worse, not better, in a lying-down posture where the arm holding the phone has less range of motion and often less strength available to reposition it. The fix is straightforward once named: move the primary action toward the bottom of the layout, or into a sticky, always-reachable position at the bottom of the screen, and let the decorative image occupy the harder-to-reach space it isn't actually doing functional work in anyway.

contentSections.body: Reachability and target size are two different problems — a button can be plenty large and still sit in the one zone of the screen a one-handed, lying-down thumb genuinely can't comfortably get to.

title: Writing an energy-cost finding that survives "that's not WCAG"
description: "That's not WCAG" is a real objection an energy-cost finding needs to survive, not a reason to soften it into vague advice — the finding that survives names a number, a specific consequence, and a concrete fix, the same as any other finding in the audit.

learningObjectives.text: Structure an energy-cost finding with a quantified cost, a specific consequence and a concrete fix
Respond to 'that's not WCAG' without either overclaiming a citation or abandoning the finding
Cite adjacent, genuinely relevant WCAG criteria without overstating what they require

contentSections.title: "That's not WCAG" is a real objection, not a bluff

contentSections.body: In a findings-review meeting, a product manager pushes back on an energy-cost finding: 'I hear you, but that's not WCAG — we're scoped to AA conformance for this audit, and I don't see a citation for "tiring to use."' They're not wrong about the citation. They're wrong that this makes the finding go away.

contentSections.question: What's the actual mistake in responding to 'that's not WCAG' by dropping the finding, versus responding by insisting (incorrectly) that it does map to a specific criterion?
contentSections.answer: Both responses are mistakes, for opposite reasons. Dropping the finding pretends a real, observed barrier stops mattering because no citation covers it — the same error this whole phase has been naming since its first module. Forcing a citation that doesn't actually fit (stretching 2.2.1 to cover something it doesn't say) undermines the audit's credibility the moment someone who knows the criterion well enough reads it closely, and it hands a skeptical reviewer an easy, legitimate reason to dismiss the whole finding. The right response says plainly: this is outside formal WCAG conformance scope, it's evaluative, and here's the evidence for why it's still real and worth fixing.
contentSections.hint: Consider what happens to the audit's credibility on every other finding, once a reviewer catches one citation that's been stretched to fit something it doesn't actually cover.

contentSections.body: This is the fourth time this phase has returned to the same underlying point, and it's worth naming why it keeps recurring: cognitive load, plain language, cumulative sensory density, and now energy cost are all real barriers WCAG's numbered criteria cover thinly or not at all, because WCAG was largely written around what could be tested mechanically at the time it was drafted. None of that makes any of them less real to the person hitting the barrier. The skill this whole phase has been building is writing a finding whose credibility comes from its evidence, not from a citation stretched to fit.
'That's not WCAG' is often true and never a reason to drop a real finding — the fix is evidence strong enough to stand without a citation, not a citation stretched to cover something it doesn't.

contentSections.title: The anatomy of a finding that holds up

contentSections.body: Two versions of the same finding about the appointment-booking flow from this module's first lesson. Version A: 'The booking flow feels tedious and could be streamlined for users with limited energy.' Version B: names the actual step count, the specific overhead steps, and the concrete consequence.

contentSections.question: Put these in the order that makes an energy-cost finding actually defensible under pushback, most load-bearing first.
steps: State the measured cost precisely — the actual interaction count, not a vague impression ('tedious', 'a lot of steps')
Name which specific steps are avoidable overhead versus genuinely essential, so the claim can be checked step by step

State the real consequence for the specific user this affects — not 'inconvenient' but what it actually costs someone with a fixed energy budget (a task not completed, a second attempt that doesn't exist today)
Propose a specific, concrete fix, and cite any genuinely adjacent WCAG criteria honestly as supporting context rather than as the finding's sole justification
contentSections.explanation: A precise count is the hardest part to argue with — 'fourteen steps, six of them essential' survives scrutiny in a way 'this feels tedious' never will, because it's checkable. Naming which specific steps are overhead turns a subjective impression into an itemised, falsifiable claim anyone can verify by walking the flow themselves. The consequence is what makes it a finding worth acting on rather than a style preference — 'inconvenient' invites a shrug, 'this person may not complete this task today at all' does not. And a concrete fix, with any real adjacent citations (2.2.1's timing requirements, 3.3.7's redundant-entry rule) named honestly for what they do and don't cover, is what turns the finding into something a team can actually act on rather than argue about.

contentSections.body: The version that survives 'that's not WCAG' in the room isn't the version with the most confident tone — it's the version built the way this whole lesson describes: a number, a named breakdown, a real consequence, a concrete fix, and total honesty about which parts are formal conformance and which parts are the evaluative judgement this whole track keeps teaching are worth making anyway.
A precise count and a specific consequence survive pushback that a vague impression never will — the finding's strength comes from being checkable, not from how confidently it's stated.

title: Practice — Count and Reduce the Interaction Cost of Seven Tasks
description: Seven drills across the module's skills. No new concepts: this is where counting a real interaction cost, and telling a genuine energy-saving fix from a cosmetic one, stops being something you've read about.

learningObjectives.text: Apply interaction-counting, redo-cost and posture judgement to unfamiliar tasks at speed
Distinguish a genuine energy-cost reduction from one that only reduces a different metric

contentSections.title: Seven drills

contentSections.body: Nothing new here. Seven drills across the module's skills, ordered from where the lessons ended to one step past it. Do them in one sitting if that works, or spread across several — the set doesn't expire and nothing is timed.
If a drill needed a hint, that's the thing to watch for in the checkpoint — not a reason to redo the set.

title: Lab — Produce an Interaction-Cost Audit of a Core User Journey
description: Pick a real, multi-step journey and produce the artefact this whole module has been building toward: an honest interaction count, the session and redo risks that actually apply, and reductions specific enough for a team to build.

learningObjectives.text: Build a complete interaction inventory for a real, multi-step journey
Evaluate session-timeout and redo-risk exposure against a real, unpredictable interruption
Write energy-cost findings precise enough to survive pushback

contentSections.title: The lab

contentSections.body: Pick a real, multi-step journey you can access today — booking something, applying for something, completing a multi-page form. This lab produces an energy-cost audit of it: an honest count, the real risks, and specific reductions, not a redesign.

contentSections.title: Energy-cost audit of a core user journey
contentSections.brief: Choose a real, multi-step journey (at least 4 distinct steps or screens) you can access with the energy you have today. Build a full interaction inventory, evaluate its session-timeout and redo-cost exposure, check its one-handed/lying-down completability, and write findings precise enough to survive 'that's not WCAG.'
contentSections.deliverable: An audit with interaction counts, session and redo risks, and concrete reductions for each finding.

stages.title: Build the interaction inventory
stages.instructions: List every tap, click or decision the journey requires, in order, without skipping the small ones. Classify each as essential or avoidable overhead. State the honest minimum count and the built count.
stages.checkpoint: You have a full, numbered inventory with each step classified, and a stated built-count versus honest-minimum gap.

stages.title: Evaluate session and redo risk
stages.instructions: Check for any session timeout — does it warn, extend, and (separately) does it autosave? Deliberately test what happens if you close the tab or lose connection partway through — does the journey resume where you left off, or restart? Note exactly what a real, unpredictable-length interruption would cost at each stage.
stages.checkpoint: You have a precise account, tested rather than assumed, of what an interruption or a crash would actually cost at each stage of the journey.

stages.title: Check one-handed and lying-down completability
stages.instructions: Identify any step requiring a sustained gesture (drag, pinch, long-press) or placing a primary action in a hard-to-reach zone for a one-handed, lying-down posture. Note each one specifically.
stages.checkpoint: Every gesture-dependent or reach-dependent step is logged with a specific alternative proposed.

stages.title: Write the findings and self-check
stages.instructions: For every finding, write it with a precise count or observation, a specific consequence, and a concrete fix — the structure from the module's final lesson. Then run the self-check below.
stages.checkpoint: Every finding has a number or specific observation, a real stated consequence, and a fix specific enough to build from.

rubric.criterion: The interaction inventory is complete and honestly counted
rubric.meets: A reader can see every step, which ones are essential, and the gap between the built count and the honest minimum.

rubric.criterion: Session and redo risk is tested, not assumed
rubric.meets: The audit states what was actually observed when a timeout or interruption was deliberately triggered, not a guess about what probably happens.

rubric.criterion: At least one one-handed or lying-down-specific finding is included
rubric.meets: A gesture or reachability problem is named with a specific, buildable alternative.

rubric.criterion: Every finding survives 'that's not WCAG'
rubric.meets: Each finding has a number, a specific consequence, and honest labelling of what's formal conformance versus evaluative judgement.

rubric.criterion: The audit reflects a real energy budget
rubric.meets: The stages were completed as separate sittings if needed — nothing about the audit required doing it in one unbroken 50-minute block.

contentSections.body: A journey you've only ever completed on a good day, at a desk, with both hands free, is a journey whose real cost to someone without those three things you don't actually know — this lab is the difference between assuming it's fine and having tested it.

title: Checkpoint — Interaction Cost: What a Task Really Demands
description: Ten questions pulling across this module, the module before it, and further back. Ungraded, untimed, and getting one wrong just means it comes back later.

learningObjectives.text: Retrieve the module's core distinctions without looking them up

contentSections.title: Let's see what stuck
Checkpoint — Interaction Cost: What a Task Really Demands

questions.from: This module — Interaction Cost: What a Task Really Demands
questions.prompt: An interaction inventory finds a task takes 14 taps as built, with a 6-tap honest minimum. What's the actual finding?

options.label: 14 is simply a lot of taps and should be reduced generally
The gap between 14 and the honestly-necessary 6 — the specific avoidable overhead steps, named individually
Nothing — 14 taps is a normal length for any real task

questions.explanation: The finding is the gap between the built count and the honest minimum, with each avoidable step named specifically — not a vague impression that the total feels high.

questions.from: This module — Interaction Cost: What a Task Really Demands
questions.prompt: A form has a warn-and-extend session timeout that comfortably satisfies WCAG 2.2.1. Why might this still fail to protect someone mid-way through a dysautonomia episode?

options.label: It can't fail — 2.2.1 compliance guarantees the data is protected
The mechanism still depends on the person being present and able to respond to the warning, which an involuntary, unpredictable-length interruption doesn't guarantee
2.2.1 doesn't apply to medical or benefits forms

questions.explanation: A warn-and-extend mechanism protects a predictable interruption where the person can act on the warning — it does nothing for an interruption that removes their ability to respond at exactly the moment the mechanism needs them to.

questions.from: This module — Interaction Cost: What a Task Really Demands
questions.prompt: Why is 'reduces how often data gets lost' (a longer timeout) a weaker claim than 'protects the data regardless of interruption length' (autosave)?

options.label: They're the same claim, just worded differently
A longer timeout only lowers the odds for people within the new limit — it doesn't remove the risk, while autosave removes it regardless of how long the interruption actually lasts
Autosave is always technically harder to build than a longer timeout

questions.explanation: Reducing frequency and removing risk entirely are different properties — a longer timeout still eventually fails someone slower or more interrupted than the new limit assumes.

questions.from: This module — Interaction Cost: What a Task Really Demands
questions.prompt: A drag-to-reorder gesture and a pair of 'move up'/'move down' buttons produce the same result. Why does the button version matter for one-handed use specifically?

options.label: Buttons are always visually larger than drag handles
A discrete tap doesn't require the device to stay steady through a sustained motion, so it doesn't silently assume a second free hand to brace the phone
Drag gestures don't work on touchscreens at all

questions.explanation: A sustained gesture requiring the phone to stay perfectly still assumes a second hand or a stable surface — a single discrete tap achieves the same outcome without either assumption.

questions.from: Previous module — Motion, Sound and Sensory Load
questions.prompt: A carousel auto-advances every 4 seconds indefinitely, alongside other page content, with no pause button. What does this fail?

options.label: Nothing — carousels are exempt from motion criteria
WCAG 2.2.2 Pause, Stop, Hide — auto-starting, running past 5 seconds, and appearing alongside other content together require a pause/stop/hide mechanism
Only a problem if it includes video

questions.explanation: All three conditions together (auto-start, past 5 seconds, parallel with other content) trigger 2.2.2's requirement for a pause control.

questions.from: Previous module — Motion, Sound and Sensory Load
questions.prompt: A CMS marks a video 'Captions: enabled' based on a file existing, though the auto-generated captions garble key terms throughout. Does this satisfy WCAG 1.2.2?

options.label: Yes — 1.2.2 only requires a captions file to exist
No — captions this inaccurate fail to convey the actual content, even with a track technically present
Yes, as long as a transcript exists separately

questions.explanation: A presence check is a different, easier question than whether the captions actually convey the audio content.

questions.from: Previous module — Motion, Sound and Sensory Load
questions.prompt: A design cleared a general flash-rate check using a placeholder gray color, then shipped in saturated red at the same rate. Why might it still fail?

options.label: Saturated red transitions have their own, stricter threshold, tested independently of the general flash check
It can't fail once the general rate passes, regardless of color
Red only matters above 10 flashes per second

questions.explanation: The red flash threshold is separate from and stricter than the general flash threshold — clearing one with a different color doesn't clear the other for the actual shipped color.

questions.from: 3+ modules back — Cognitive Accessibility
questions.prompt: A billing address field is left blank with no checkbox to reuse the shipping address entered two screens earlier. What does this violate?

options.label: WCAG 3.3.7 Redundant Entry — no mechanism to reuse or auto-populate the earlier value
Nothing, since the user already typed the address once
WCAG 2.1.2 No Keyboard Trap

questions.explanation: 3.3.7 requires information already provided to be auto-populated or available to select, not simply theoretically re-typeable by the user.

questions.from: 3+ modules back — Cognitive Accessibility
questions.prompt: A one-time verification code field blocks paste, forcing the code to be retyped from memory after switching apps. Why does this tend to increase errors?

options.label: It forces manual retention and retyping across an app switch — exactly the condition most likely to produce a transposed digit
Paste never works reliably on mobile devices anyway
It doesn't — this is a myth

questions.explanation: The failure mode blocking paste prevents is minor; the failure mode it guarantees — retyping a number from memory under time pressure — is the larger one.

questions.from: 3+ modules back — Cognitive Accessibility
questions.prompt: A form clears a CVV field after a declined payment, and also clears the correctly-entered shipping address on the same page. What's the right read?

options.label: Both are defensible — any failed submission should clear all fields
Clearing the CVV is a defensible security choice; clearing the unrelated shipping address is a state-management defect with no equivalent justification
Neither should ever be cleared under any circumstances

questions.explanation: A narrow, real security reason can justify not retaining one specific sensitive value — it never justifies clearing unrelated correct fields alongside it.

contentSections.body: None of these need to be perfect. What matters is which ones needed a guess — that's what the next checkpoint will bring back.

title: Forms that demand more than they need
description: A mental-health app that requires a mandatory free-text 'reason for signing up' before letting anyone in crisis reach a single resource is asking someone to narrate their pain to a form before it will help them — and 'we might need this data someday' is not the same claim as 'this task needs it right now.'

learningObjectives.text: Evaluate whether a requested field is actually required for the task in front of the user
Identify 'just in case' data collection and its real, specific costs
Propose a narrower field or mechanism that achieves the same legitimate purpose

contentSections.title: The form that makes you explain yourself before it helps you

contentSections.body: A mental-health support app's signup screen has one mandatory field before anything else is reachable: a free-text box labelled 'Tell us why you're here today,' with no skip option and no character limit stated. Someone signing up mid-crisis, looking for the fastest path to a crisis line number, has to compose a written account of what's wrong before the app will show them anything at all.

contentSections.scenario: The product team's stated reason for this field is 'so we can personalise the experience.' Personalisation could plausibly use this information, but the immediate task — getting a person in crisis to a resource — doesn't require it at all.
contentSections.question: What's the right way to evaluate this field?

options.label: It's justified, because personalisation is a legitimate product goal

The stated purpose (personalisation) doesn't require this field to be mandatory or to gate access to anything — the actual test is whether the immediate task in front of the user needs it, and finding a crisis resource doesn't
It's fine as long as the field is optional to fill in, regardless of whether it's mandatory to skip

feedback.justified: A legitimate long-term goal doesn't automatically justify making a field mandatory at this specific moment, in this specific task — personalisation could happen later, optionally, once the person has actually reached the help they came for.
feedback.gate: Right. The question isn't whether this information could ever be useful to the product — it's whether the task the person is actually trying to complete right now requires it. Gating access to a crisis resource behind a mandatory disclosure fails that test even if the disclosure itself would be reasonable as an optional, later step.
feedback.confused: A mandatory field that blocks access is the actual problem here — whether it's technically possible to type nothing isn't the same as whether the interface actually lets you proceed without typing something.

contentSections.concept: **The right test for any requested field is whether the task in front of the user, right now, actually requires it — not whether the organisation could someday find a use for it.** 'We might need this' and 'this task needs this' are different claims, and conflating them is how forms accumulate fields nobody individually decided were essential. A mandatory disclosure gating access to help is a more serious version of the same failure than an optional one that can be skipped and returned to.

contentSections.body: The practical test worth applying to every field on a form, one at a time: could you explain, out loud, to the actual person filling this in, exactly why you need this specific piece of information for the task they're trying to complete right now? 'So we can personalise things later' is a real answer to a different question — it doesn't survive being asked about a field gating access to an urgent, time-sensitive resource.

The fix here isn't necessarily deleting the field — personalisation data can be genuinely useful. It's sequencing: let the person reach what they came for first, then ask, optionally, once they're not blocked by it. A field's necessity is not a fixed property; it changes with when and how it's asked, which is exactly why the same question ('why are you here today?') can be reasonable as an optional follow-up and harmful as a mandatory gate.

'We might use this data eventually' and 'this task needs it right now' are different claims — a field that fails the second test shouldn't gate access to the task, even if it might survive as an optional, later ask.

contentSections.title: Date of birth, when 'are you over 18' would do

contentSections.body: A job application asks for full date of birth, explained internally as 'we need to verify the applicant meets the legal working age.' The application form also asks for marital status and a photo upload, with no stated purpose given for either.

contentSections.scenario: Verifying someone is over the legal working age genuinely requires knowing whether they're over a threshold. It does not require knowing their exact birth date, which additionally exposes their precise age to whoever reviews the application.
contentSections.question: What's the actual mechanism that makes the exact-date-of-birth field a problem here, given the stated purpose is legitimate?

options.label: Age verification is being solved with a field that collects far more than the stated purpose requires — exposing exact birthdate creates a real, specific age-discrimination exposure a simple threshold checkbox wouldn't
Nothing — any information a company might act on responsibly is fine to collect
The problem is only that the field is labelled unclearly

feedback.fine: 'Might act on it responsibly' isn't the standard — the field itself creates real exposure the moment it exists, regardless of anyone's stated intentions, because it puts information in front of a reviewer that a narrower field never would have.
feedback.overcollect: Right. 'Are you over the legal working age? (yes/no)' verifies exactly what the stated purpose requires, with nothing extra. An exact date of birth verifies the same threshold while additionally exposing precise age to a hiring reviewer — creating a real, specific, avoidable age-discrimination risk the stated purpose never actually needed.
feedback.label: Clearer labelling wouldn't change what information the field actually collects or exposes — the problem is the field's scope, not how it's described.

contentSections.mechanism: **A field that collects more than its stated purpose requires creates exposure the purpose never justified.** A threshold check ('are you over X') and an exact value ('what is your date of birth') can serve the identical stated purpose while exposing very different amounts of information to whoever sees the answer — the narrower version is very often just as functional and meaningfully safer. This is worth checking on every field with a 'we need this to verify something' justification: does verifying it actually require the exact value, or just where it falls relative to a line?

contentSections.body: The same test applied to the marital-status and photo fields on the same application finds no stated purpose at all for either — which is its own, even more direct finding: a field with no articulable reason for existing is the clearest case of 'we might need this someday' standing in for an actual justification, and it's worth naming as its own separate line item rather than lumping it in with the birthdate field's narrower, more defensible-sounding problem.

A threshold question and an exact value can serve the same stated purpose while exposing very different amounts of information — asking whether the exact value is actually required, or just a line to fall on either side of, catches over-collection a purpose-based justification alone won't.

title: Disclosure, medical questions and who sees the answer
description: A conference's 'accessibility needs' field, forwarded unfiltered into a shared spreadsheet every volunteer with a badge scanner can open, turns a reasonable question into a real disclosure of medical information to people who never needed to know it.

learningObjectives.text: Evaluate whether a disclosure request is scoped to who actually needs the information
Diagnose how a reasonable question becomes a real disclosure harm through its routing, not its wording
Distinguish a need-to-know-scoped request from an unfiltered broadcast of sensitive information

contentSections.title: The accessibility question that ends up in everyone's inbox

contentSections.body: A conference's registration form asks: 'Do you have any accessibility needs we should know about?' — a reasonable, well-intentioned question. The answer, submitted as free text, is compiled automatically into a single spreadsheet shared with every volunteer, badge-scanning staff member, and vendor with event-day access, none of whom individually needed to see any specific attendee's medical information to do their job.

contentSections.scenario: The question itself is reasonable to ask. The routing sends every answer to a wide, undifferentiated group with event-day access, rather than to whoever specifically needs to act on each particular need.
contentSections.question: What's the actual failure here — the question, or something else?

options.label: The question itself — accessibility needs should never be asked about at all

The routing — a reasonable question becomes a real disclosure harm once the answer reaches a wide group with no individual need to know it, rather than only the specific staff who'll act on each request
Nothing is wrong — any staff member might need this information at some point

feedback.question: Asking about accessibility needs is genuinely useful and often necessary for an organiser to actually provide accommodations — removing the question entirely would make the event less accessible, not more dignified.
feedback.routing: Right. The question is fine; the failure is that every answer reaches everyone with event-day system access, rather than only the specific person or team who needs to know a particular attendee needs, say, a step-free route or a quiet room. Disclosure harm here comes from breadth of access, not from the question having been asked at all.
feedback.nothing: 'Might need it at some point' is exactly the 'just in case' justification from the previous lesson, applied to routing instead of collection — a hypothetical future need doesn't justify a wide group having access to sensitive information today.

contentSections.concept: **A disclosure question can be entirely reasonable and still cause real harm through how the answer is routed.** The relevant question isn't only 'should we ask this' — it's 'who specifically needs to see this answer to act on it, and does our system actually limit access to that group, or does it broadcast to everyone with general system access because narrower routing was more engineering work.' A wellintentioned question with unscoped routing produces the same harm as a badly-worded one.

contentSections.body: This is the same shape of problem as a WCAG finding about redundant entry or an energy-cost finding about unnecessary steps — a specific, checkable, fixable defect, not a vague sense that 'privacy matters.' The fix is concrete: route each disclosure only to the specific role that acts on it (a step-free route request goes to the venue-logistics contact, a quiet-room request goes to whoever manages that space), with no default access for anyone outside that specific need, and log who has actually viewed a given disclosure.
A reasonable question and unscoped routing combine to create a real disclosure harm — the fix targets who can see the answer, not whether the question should have been asked.

contentSections.title: One shared inbox versus the person who actually needs to know

contentSections.body: A university's disability-accommodations request form sends every submission — exam extensions, note-taker requests, medical details supporting each request — to one shared departmental inbox, checked by whichever administrative staff member happens to be covering the desk that day, rather than to the specific disability-services coordinator whose job is actually to process them.

contentSections.scenario: The shared inbox exists because it was simpler to build than a routing system directing requests to a specific role — 'someone will see it and forward it along' was the reasoning.
contentSections.question: What's the actual mechanism making the shared inbox a real problem, beyond general inconvenience?

options.label: Whoever happens to be covering the desk that day sees detailed medical information they have no operational need to know, purely because scoped routing wasn't built — the same state-management-shortcut pattern from an earlier module's form-clearing finding, applied to who sees sensitive data instead of what data survives an error
Nothing — administrative staff are bound by general confidentiality expectations, so this is fine
The problem is only that requests might get lost or delayed, not who sees them

feedback.fine: A general expectation of professionalism isn't the same protection as a system that only shows sensitive information to the specific person who needs it to do their job — the harm here is structural (unnecessary exposure by default), not a claim that any specific staff member will misuse it.
feedback.sameashortcut: Right. This is the same underlying pattern as the earlier module's form that clears every field on one field's error — a broad, undifferentiated default ('the whole form resets' / 'everyone in the shared inbox sees it') chosen because it was easier to build than the narrower, correct version ('only the failed field resets' / 'only the coordinator sees it').
feedback.delayonly: Delay is a real, separate problem worth its own finding, but it doesn't address the exposure question — even a request processed instantly still exposed detailed medical information to whichever staff member happened to open the inbox first.

contentSections.mechanism: **A shared, undifferentiated destination for sensitive information is very often a state-management shortcut wearing a privacy problem's clothes — the broad default exists because building narrower routing was more work, not because broad access was actually intended or needed.** The fix pattern is the same one this whole phase keeps returning to at different scales: route to the specific, narrow destination that actually needs the information, rather than a wide default nobody individually decided was correct.

contentSections.body: The honest caveat worth naming in a finding like this: sometimes a small organisation genuinely doesn't have the staffing to build role-specific routing, and 'one inbox, one trusted person' is a real, defensible interim state — the actual test is whether access is scoped to as narrow a group as the organisation's real structure allows, not whether it's perfectly scoped in the abstract. A five-person nonprofit's single coordinator inbox is a different finding than a large university routing sensitive requests to whoever's covering a shared desk.

Broad, unscoped access to sensitive disclosures is usually a shortcut, not a decision — the fix routes each disclosure to the specific role that acts on it, scaled honestly to what the organisation can actually build.

title: Dark patterns aimed at people who are tired
description: A six-screen cancellation flow — two retention offers, a mandatory survey, confirmshaming copy on every decline button — isn't badly designed by accident. It's built on the specific bet that enough tired people will give up before screen six, and for someone on a fixed energy budget, giving up mid-task is the literal, designed outcome.

learningObjectives.text: Identify named dark-pattern types (roach motel, confirmshaming, forced continuity) from real interface copy and flow structure
Explain why staged, multi-screen friction specifically exploits fatigue as an attack surface
Document a dark-pattern flow completely enough for the finding to be undeniable

contentSections.title: Two named patterns, in real copy

contentSections.body: A fitness app's cancellation flow: tapping 'Cancel Subscription' opens a screen reading '50% off for 3 months, just for you!' with two buttons — a large colored 'Claim my discount' and, underneath in small gray text, 'No thanks, I'll keep paying full price.' Declining that opens a second screen: 'Before you go — here's everything you'll lose,' followed by a bulleted feature list, a large 'Stay subscribed' button, and a small gray text link reading 'Continue cancelling.' Declining that opens a mandatory 'Why are you leaving?' dropdown with no way to skip it. Only after all three screens does an actual cancel button appear.

contentSections.scenario: This flow uses two named, well-documented dark-pattern types: confirmshaming (loaded language on the decline option, like 'I'll keep paying full price,' designed to make the honest choice feel foolish) and roach motel (easy to get in, deliberately hard to get out).
contentSections.question: Is this legitimate retention UX, or a dark pattern — and what's the actual test?

options.label: Legitimate — any company is entitled to try to retain a customer before they leave

A dark pattern — the test isn't whether retention offers exist at all, it's whether the flow is staged specifically to maximise how many people give up before completing an action they've already clearly stated they want, using loaded language and escalating friction rather than a single clear offer and a respected decision
It depends entirely on the size of the discount offered

feedback.legit: A single, clearly-presented retention offer, with a plainly labelled 'no thanks' that doesn't editorialise the user's choice, is genuinely legitimate business behaviour. This flow goes well past that: multiple staged screens, loaded decline copy, and a mandatory survey blocking the actual cancel button are specifically about attrition through friction, not one honest offer.
feedback.dark: Right. The test isn't 'did they try to keep the customer' — it's whether the flow is engineered to make giving up easier than finishing, using loaded language on the honest choice and escalating friction rather than a single respected decision. Two named patterns are both present here: confirmshaming (the decline copy) and roach motel (the multi-screen structure making exit harder than entry).
feedback.discount: The discount's size doesn't change the structure of the flow — a 90% discount offer inside the exact same six-screen, confirmshamed, mandatory-survey structure would still be the same dark pattern, just a more generous version of it.

contentSections.concept: **Confirmshaming and roach motel are specific, named, well-documented dark patterns, not vague complaints about 'annoying UX.'** Confirmshaming uses loaded language on the option someone didn't want to choose, designed to make it feel foolish or ungrateful to select ('No thanks, I don't want to save money'). Roach motel makes entry effortless and exit deliberately, disproportionately harder than entry ever was. Naming which specific pattern is present, with the actual copy quoted, turns 'this feels manipulative' into a specific, checkable claim a reviewer can verify by reading the same screens.

contentSections.body: The specific copy matters for the finding, not just the existence of a retention offer: 'No thanks, I'll keep paying full price' is worded to imply financial foolishness, not to neutrally describe declining an offer — a genuinely neutral version would read 'No thanks' or 'Continue cancelling' with no editorial framing at all. Quoting the actual loaded phrase, word for word, is what makes a confirmshaming finding immediately legible to anyone reading the audit, without needing to take the auditor's characterisation on faith.

Confirmshaming and roach motel are specific, named patterns with checkable definitions — quoting the actual loaded copy and counting the actual screens turns a feeling into a finding nobody can wave away as subjective.

contentSections.title: Testing the flow that's built to outlast you

contentSections.body: You're auditing the cancellation flow above for a product team who insists it's 'just a retention flow, nothing weird.' Every decision about how to test it changes what you'll actually be able to prove.

contentSections.title: Testing a cancellation flow built to outlast a tired user
contentSections.opening: You click 'Cancel Subscription' on the fitness app account settings page. The first retention screen appears: '50% off for 3 months, just for you!' with 'Claim my discount' in large color, and 'No thanks, I'll keep paying full price' in small gray text underneath.

start.situation: You've logged the confirmshaming copy on the decline button. The actual cancel action is still nowhere in sight.
start.question: What's the right next move as the auditor?

choices.label: Decline the offer and keep going, logging each screen as you go
choices.consequence: You register the pattern precisely and keep moving — the audit needs to see the whole path, not just the first recognisable pattern, to know how severe this actually is.

choices.label: Log this single screen as the complete finding and stop testing here, since the pattern is already clearly identifiable

second_offer.situation: A second screen appears: 'Before you go — here's everything you'll lose,' a bulleted feature list, a large 'Stay subscribed' button, and a small gray text link reading 'Continue cancelling.'
second_offer.question: This is screen two of an unknown total. What now?

choices.label: Continue cancelling, and keep documenting each screen precisely
choices.consequence: You're building an exact, screen-by-screen record — the kind of evidence that survives a product team's 'that's an exaggeration' pushback.

choices.label: Simulate what a genuinely fatigued user would actually do at this point, and stop here, logging the give-up itself as data

mandatory_survey.situation: A mandatory 'Why are you leaving?' dropdown blocks further progress with no way to skip it. Selecting an option finally reveals an actual, unambiguous 'Cancel my subscription' button — six screens after the original tap.
mandatory_survey.question: You've now reached the real cancel action. What's the last step of a defensible audit?

choices.label: Complete the cancellation, and write the finding with the exact screen count, the exact copy, and a comparison to a legitimate one-click cancellation

stopped_early.summary: You accurately caught the confirmshaming language on the first screen, but stopping there means the audit never discovers this is the first of six deliberately staged screens — and the finding's actual severity depends entirely on that number, which you don't yet have.
stopped_early.lesson: A single dark-pattern screen and a six-screen staged sequence are different severities of the same underlying pattern. The audit needs the whole path, not just the first recognisable instance of it.

gave_up_as_data.summary: Simulating a genuinely fatigued user's decision to give up mid-flow, and logging that give-up as real evidence, is a legitimate and specific way to demonstrate the pattern's actual cost. On its own, though, it doesn't give the audit an exact map of how many screens exist or what each one does — evidence a skeptical product team will ask for directly.
gave_up_as_data.lesson: Modelling real user fatigue is valid, additional evidence — it isn't a substitute for a complete, exact map of the flow. A strong audit does both.

full_finding.summary: You completed the flow, counted six screens total (two retention offers, a mandatory survey, then the real cancel button), and can now write a finding with an exact screen count, the exact loaded copy quoted verbatim, and a direct comparison to what a one-click cancellation would look like.
full_finding.lesson: The complete, exact path is the evidence. 'Six screens, two named dark patterns, one mandatory survey, verbatim copy attached' is a finding nobody can dismiss as an overreaction — a vague impression is exactly what invites that dismissal.

contentSections.body: The mechanism worth stating explicitly in any finding like this: staged, multi-screen friction isn't just generically annoying, it's specifically engineered around a person's declining willingness to keep clicking — and for someone managing a fixed, non-renewable daily energy budget, 'give up and stay subscribed because there's no capacity left to click through four more screens today' isn't a hypothetical edge case, it's the literal, designed outcome the flow is built to produce. This is the sharpest version yet of a pattern this whole track keeps returning to: a barrier that costs everyone something costs a person with less to spend disproportionately more, right up to costing them the outcome the flow was built to prevent.

Multi-screen retention friction doesn't just annoy people — it specifically bets on fatigue, and for someone with a fixed energy budget, giving up mid-flow isn't an edge case, it's the outcome the flow was built to produce.

title: Language that blames the user for a system failure
description: 'Your session expired due to inactivity' is a lie when the actual bug is that the form only counts mouse movement as activity and never registers a single keystroke — and the difference between a wrong message and a blaming one is exactly the difference between an inconvenience and a dignity cost.

learningObjectives.text: Distinguish a message that blames the user from one that merely lacks detail
Diagnose a system failure mislabelled as user error
Rewrite blaming or misattributed system copy toward accuracy and away from blame

contentSections.title: "Due to inactivity" — while actively typing the whole time

contentSections.body: A benefits application shows: 'Your session has expired due to inactivity.' The user had been continuously typing for the entire session, filling in long-form answers about their own medical history. The actual cause, invisible to them, is a bug: the session tracker only resets its timer on mouse movement or click events, never on keystrokes — so someone typing steadily with their hands never on the mouse looks, to the system, exactly like someone who walked away.

contentSections.scenario: The message states a specific, confident cause ('due to inactivity') that is factually false for this user — they were never inactive. The real cause is a tracking bug in the system, not anything the user did.
contentSections.question: What's the actual problem with this message, beyond simply being wrong?

options.label: It's just an inaccurate technical detail, no different in kind from any other minor bug

It confidently attributes a system failure to the user's own behaviour ('due to inactivity'), which is a specific, false accusation, not merely an unhelpful or vague message — the user did nothing wrong and is being told, in effect, that they did
The wording is fine; the problem is only that the session length itself is too short

feedback.minor: This isn't a neutral, minor inaccuracy — it's a confident, specific claim about the user's own behaviour ('due to inactivity') that's false, which is a materially different and worse failure than a message that's merely vague or unhelpful.
feedback.blame: Right. This message doesn't just fail to explain what happened — it actively misattributes a system bug to something the user is being told they did. For someone who was working hard, in good faith, on something genuinely difficult (their own medical history), being falsely told they were inactive is a real dignity cost stacked on top of the actual functional failure.
feedback.length: Session length is a separate, real issue worth its own finding — it doesn't address the specific harm of confidently, falsely blaming the user for something a system bug actually caused.

contentSections.concept: **A message that states a specific, false cause for a system's own failure is doing something worse than being unhelpful — it's assigning blame that belongs to the system onto the person who did nothing wrong.** This is a sharper version of the vague-error problem from an earlier module: 'Invalid password' with no detail is unhelpful; 'Your session expired due to inactivity' when the user was never inactive is unhelpful *and* false *and* blaming, three separate, stacking failures in one sentence.

contentSections.body: The honest, defensible version of this message states only what the system can actually verify, without inventing a cause: 'Your session ended. Your answers weren't saved — we're sorry.' This doesn't claim to know why (which the message writer, in the general case, may not), and critically doesn't attribute the ending to anything the user did. It's a smaller, more honest claim than 'due to inactivity' — and it happens to also be less wrong, because it isn't asserting a specific cause the writer can't actually verify in every case.

A message that confidently states a false cause for a system's own failure isn't just unhelpful, it's blaming — the honest fix states only what's actually known, without inventing a cause that happens to point at the user.

contentSections.title: "Please check your details" during an outage

contentSections.body: A checkout page shows 'Payment declined. Please check your card details and try again' during a two-hour outage at the payment processor, affecting every transaction on the site, not this one specific card. Dozens of customers, each individually told to check their own details, are independently re-entering correct information over and over against a system that's failing for a completely unrelated reason.

contentSections.question: What's the actual harm in this specific message, beyond it simply being inaccurate?
contentSections.answer: It individually blames each customer for a shared, systemic failure that has nothing to do with any of their card details — sending someone to re-check and re-enter information that was correct the whole time, potentially several times, while quietly hiding a real outage that has nothing to do with them. Beyond the wasted effort, it's a specific kind of gaslighting-adjacent harm: the system is confidently telling someone their own correct information is wrong, when the actual fault is entirely on the other side.
contentSections.hint: Think about what a customer is being asked to do (re-check their own correct information) versus what would actually resolve the problem (the outage ending) — and what it does to someone to be repeatedly, confidently told they made a mistake they didn't make.

contentSections.body: The general pattern worth naming across both examples in this lesson: any error message asserting a specific cause needs to actually know that cause, not guess at the most common one and present it as fact. A payment failure during a known processor outage should say something the system can actually verify — 'We're having trouble processing payments right now. This isn't something wrong with your card — please try again in a few minutes' — which is both more honest and, not incidentally, less likely to cost the business a customer who gives up after 'fixing' correct information three times in a row.

An error message that confidently names a specific cause has to actually know that cause — guessing at the most common one and blaming the user for it repeats a real harm across every person who hits the same systemic failure.

title: Accessible and still degrading: naming it in an audit
description: A benefits-screening kiosk in a public waiting room can be fully keyboard operable, perfectly labelled for a screen reader, and still force someone to state 'I am unable to work due to disability' out loud to a support worker standing beside them because the kiosk has no privacy screen — passing every conformance check while failing the person completely.

learningObjectives.text: Identify a design that's technically accessible and still humiliating or coercive
Write a dignity-focused finding with the same rigor as a conformance finding
Distinguish formal accessibility conformance from the separate, real question of dignity

contentSections.title: Every box checked, and still degrading

contentSections.body: A benefits-eligibility screening kiosk stands in the open lobby of a busy public office, no privacy screen or partition around it. It's keyboard operable, screen-reader labelled correctly, contrast-compliant, and every field passes its own WCAG check individually. One mandatory checkbox, in full public view of the queue and any staff walking past, reads: 'I confirm I am unable to work due to my disability.'

contentSections.scenario: An automated accessibility scan and a manual conformance check both return a clean pass on this kiosk.
contentSections.question: Which of these are real, additional problems the conformance pass doesn't capture? Select all that apply.

items.label: The kiosk's physical placement forces a highly personal disclosure to happen in full public view, with no privacy screen or partition of any kind
The mandatory checkbox's exact wording forces the user to personally assert a specific, stigmatised statement about themselves, rather than confirming a more neutral eligibility fact
The checkbox text fails contrast requirements
The checkbox isn't properly exposed to a screen reader

explanation.no-privacy: Yes — this is a real, physical-environment finding entirely outside what any conformance scan measures: the interface can be perfectly built and still force a personal disclosure into public view because of where and how it's physically deployed.
explanation.phrasing: Yes — the specific words a person is required to personally affirm matter independently of the interface's technical correctness; a more neutral, functionally equivalent phrasing ('I meet the eligibility criteria for this benefit') could confirm the identical fact without requiring the user to personally declare a stigmatised self-description out loud or on a screen others can see.
explanation.contrast: This scenario states the checkbox passes contrast requirements — the finding here isn't a conformance failure at all, it's a separate, real problem the passing conformance check doesn't reach.
explanation.screenreader: Same as contrast — the scenario states this passes screen-reader labelling correctly. The two real problems in this scenario are not conformance failures; they exist alongside a clean conformance pass.

contentSections.synthesis: Both real problems here sit entirely outside what a conformance audit measures, and that's the point: an interface can pass every individual accessibility check and still be genuinely degrading to use, through its physical deployment context or through the specific words it forces someone to personally affirm. Neither of these is a WCAG failure, and neither is any less real or less worth fixing for that.

contentSections.body: This is the sharpest version of the honest-limits pattern this whole phase has built toward: WCAG conformance and dignity are genuinely separate axes, and a perfect score on one says nothing about the other. A good audit reports both, clearly labelled as what they are — this is a real, important distinction to hold, not a reason to treat dignity findings as somehow softer or less rigorous than conformance ones.

Conformance and dignity are separate axes — an interface can pass every accessibility check and still force a humiliating disclosure through its physical placement or its exact wording, and that's a real, separate finding, not a lesser one.

contentSections.title: Writing the finding with the same rigor as any other

contentSections.body: A junior reviewer drafts this finding: 'The kiosk feels dehumanizing and should be redesigned to be more respectful.' It's accurate in spirit and won't survive a single round of pushback from a team that (correctly) points out the kiosk passes every conformance check they were scoped to meet.

contentSections.question: Put these in the order that makes a dignity finding as rigorous and defensible as any conformance finding.
steps: Describe the specific, observable fact — the physical placement, the exact wording, the exact moment of exposure — not a general impression
State plainly that this sits outside formal WCAG conformance scope, so the finding isn't mistaken for an unsupported conformance claim
Name the specific, concrete harm to the specific person in this specific situation, not a general claim about dignity
Propose a specific, implementable fix — a privacy screen, a rephrased checkbox — the same way any other finding in the audit does
contentSections.explanation: Starting with the specific, observable fact (no privacy screen, the exact checkbox wording) is what makes the finding checkable by anyone who visits the kiosk, the same standard a conformance finding is held to. Being explicit that this sits outside formal conformance scope protects the finding's credibility — it isn't overclaiming a citation, and it isn't apologising for not having one either. Naming the specific harm to this specific situation (a public disclosure of a stigmatised status, forced by the environment) is what turns 'feels dehumanizing' into an argument someone has to actually engage with rather than dismiss as a feeling. And a concrete fix is what makes the finding actionable rather than a complaint with nowhere to go.

contentSections.body: The rewritten version: *The eligibility-confirmation kiosk is deployed in the open lobby with no privacy screen or partition, requiring users to check a box stating 'I confirm I am unable to work due to my disability' in full view of the queue and passing staff. This sits outside formal WCAG conformance scope — the interface itself is correctly built and passes every conformance check — but is a real, specific dignity harm: a stigmatised personal disclosure forced into public view by the kiosk's physical placement and the checkbox's exact wording. Recommend: a privacy screen or partition around the kiosk, and rephrasing the checkbox to confirm eligibility functionally ('I meet the eligibility criteria for this benefit') without requiring the user to personally declare a stigmatised self-description.* This version survives the exact pushback the first draft couldn't.

A dignity finding built from a specific observable fact, honest labelling of its conformance status, a named concrete harm, and a specific fix is exactly as rigorous as any conformance finding — and survives the same pushback.

title: Practice — Judge Eight Designs for Dignity as Well as Conformance
description: Eight drills across the module's skills. No new concepts: this is where telling a genuine dark pattern from ordinary retention UX, and a real disclosure harm from an over-cautious complaint, stops being something you've read about.

learningObjectives.text: Apply data-minimisation, disclosure-routing, dark-pattern and blame-language judgement to unfamiliar designs at speed
Distinguish a genuine dignity finding from an overreach or an unfixable conformance-adjacent complaint

contentSections.title: Eight drills

contentSections.body: Nothing new here. Eight drills across the module's skills, ordered from where the lessons ended to one step past it. Do them in one sitting if that works, or spread across several — the set doesn't expire and nothing is timed.
If a drill needed a hint, that's the thing to watch for in the checkpoint — not a reason to redo the set.

title: Lab — Review a Sensitive Intake Flow
description: Pick a real flow that collects personal or sensitive information and review it for data minimisation, disclosure routing, dark patterns and blame language — the full set this module has been building toward, applied to one real, consequential flow.

learningObjectives.text: Evaluate a real intake flow's field-by-field necessity and disclosure routing
Identify any dark-pattern structure or blaming system language present
Write dignity-focused findings with concrete, implementable alternatives

contentSections.title: The lab

contentSections.body: Pick a real intake, signup, application or cancellation flow you can access today — a healthcare portal, a benefits application, a subscription's cancel flow, an event registration collecting accessibility or medical information. This lab produces a dignity review of it, naming every unnecessary disclosure and coercive pattern with a specific alternative for each.

contentSections.title: Dignity review of a sensitive intake flow
contentSections.brief: Choose a real flow that collects personal, medical, or otherwise sensitive information, or a cancellation/decline flow. Review every field for necessity, every sensitive answer for where it's routed, the full flow for any dark-pattern structure, and any system messaging for blame language.
contentSections.deliverable: A review naming every unnecessary disclosure and coercive pattern, with alternatives.

stages.title: Field-by-field necessity and routing
stages.instructions: For every field collecting personal or sensitive information, ask: does the immediate task actually require this, or just a narrower version of it (a threshold instead of an exact value)? Where the answer goes somewhere after submission, note who actually receives or can see it, and whether that's scoped to who needs to know.
stages.checkpoint: Every sensitive field has a necessity note and, where determinable, a routing note.

stages.title: Dark-pattern and friction audit
stages.instructions: If the flow includes any decline, cancel, or opt-out path, walk it completely and document every screen, exact button copy, and any mandatory step blocking completion. Name any specific pattern present (confirmshaming, roach motel, forced continuity) with the exact copy quoted.
stages.checkpoint: Any friction path is fully mapped with an exact screen count and exact quoted copy, not a general impression.

stages.title: Blame-language and dignity pass, findings, self-check
stages.instructions: Check any error or system message for whether it states a cause it can actually verify, and whether that cause implicates the user. Separately, evaluate the flow's physical or contextual deployment (if applicable) and any required self-descriptions for dignity, independent of conformance. Write every finding with a specific fact, honest conformance-status labelling, a named harm, and a concrete fix. Then run the self-check below.
stages.checkpoint: Every finding has a specific fact, a stated conformance status, a named harm, and a concrete, implementable fix.

rubric.criterion: Every sensitive field is checked against the task's actual necessity, not just its stated purpose
rubric.meets: A reader can see, for each flagged field, why a narrower version would or wouldn't serve the same purpose.

rubric.criterion: Any friction or decline path is fully and exactly documented
rubric.meets: The audit includes an exact screen count and quoted copy for any dark-pattern finding, not a general impression.

rubric.criterion: Blame language is checked for verifiability, not just tone
rubric.meets: At least one finding states whether a message's claimed cause is something the system can actually verify.

rubric.criterion: Every dignity finding is as rigorous as a conformance finding
rubric.meets: Each has a specific fact, honest conformance-status labelling, a named harm, and a concrete fix.

rubric.criterion: The review reflects a real energy budget
rubric.meets: The stages were completed as separate sittings if needed — nothing about the review required one unbroken 50-minute block.

contentSections.body: A flow that's never been reviewed for dignity, only for conformance, is a flow whose real cost to the person using it at their most vulnerable moment is still unknown — this lab is the difference between assuming it's respectful and having checked.

title: Checkpoint — Trauma-Informed and Dignity-Preserving Design
description: Ten questions pulling across this module, the module before it, and further back. Ungraded, untimed, and getting one wrong just means it comes back later.

learningObjectives.text: Retrieve the module's core distinctions without looking them up

contentSections.title: Let's see what stuck
Checkpoint — Trauma-Informed and Dignity-Preserving Design

questions.from: This module — Trauma-Informed and Dignity-Preserving Design
questions.prompt: A mental-health app requires a mandatory free-text 'reason for signing up' field before showing any resource. What's the right test for this field?

options.label: Whether the organisation could someday find a use for this data

Whether the immediate task the person is trying to complete right now actually requires it — gating access to a crisis resource behind a disclosure fails this even if the disclosure could be reasonable as a later, optional ask
Whether the field is technically possible to leave blank

questions.explanation: 'We might use this eventually' and 'this task needs it right now' are different claims — the field's necessity depends on the task in front of the user, not a hypothetical future use.

questions.from: This module — Trauma-Informed and Dignity-Preserving Design
questions.prompt: A conference's accessibility-needs question is reasonable, but every answer is visible to any volunteer with event-day system access. What's the actual failure?

options.label: The question itself, which should never be asked
The routing — a reasonable question becomes a real disclosure harm once the answer reaches a wide group with no individual need to know it
Nothing — any staff member might eventually need the information

questions.explanation: A well-intentioned question with unscoped routing produces the same harm as a badly-worded one — the fix targets who can see the answer, not whether the question should exist.

questions.from: This module — Trauma-Informed and Dignity-Preserving Design
questions.prompt: A cancellation flow's decline button reads 'No thanks, I'll keep paying full price.' What is this specific pattern called?

options.label: Roach motel
Confirmshaming — loaded language on the option someone didn't want, designed to make it feel foolish
Forced continuity

questions.explanation: Confirmshaming uses loaded language on the decline option specifically — a neutral version would read 'No thanks' or 'Continue cancelling' with no editorial framing.

questions.from: This module — Trauma-Informed and Dignity-Preserving Design
questions.prompt: A message reads 'Your session expired due to inactivity' for a user who was typing continuously. What makes this worse than a merely vague error message?

options.label: It's the same severity as any vague message
It confidently states a specific, false cause that blames the user for a system bug they didn't cause — a more serious, stacking failure than simply lacking detail
The only problem is that the session length is too short

questions.explanation: A confidently stated, false, blaming cause is a materially worse failure than a vague one — it's unhelpful, false, and blaming all at once.

questions.from: Previous module — Interaction Cost: What a Task Really Demands
questions.prompt: A form has a warn-and-extend session timeout that fully satisfies WCAG 2.2.1. Why might this still fail to protect someone mid-episode of an involuntary health event?

options.label: It can't fail if 2.2.1 is met
The mechanism still depends on the person being present and able to respond to the warning, which an unpredictable, involuntary interruption doesn't guarantee
2.2.1 doesn't apply to medical or benefits forms

questions.explanation: A warn-and-extend mechanism protects a predictable interruption where the person can act on the warning — it does nothing for one that removes their ability to respond.

questions.from: Previous module — Interaction Cost: What a Task Really Demands
questions.prompt: A five-page form saves nothing until final submission. A failure on page 4 costs how much work?

options.label: Only the unsaved fields on page 4
All four completed pages equally, regardless of how much was actually finished
Nothing — most forms autosave by default

questions.explanation: With no intermediate saving, a failure at any point costs everything completed up to that point equally — per-page or per-field saving bounds this loss to a much smaller unit of work.

questions.from: Previous module — Interaction Cost: What a Task Really Demands
questions.prompt: A drag-to-reorder gesture and a pair of 'move up'/'move down' buttons produce the same result. Why does the button version matter for one-handed use?

options.label: Buttons are always visually larger
A discrete tap doesn't require the device to stay steady through a sustained motion, so it doesn't silently assume a second free hand
Drag gestures don't work on touchscreens

questions.explanation: A sustained gesture requiring the phone to stay perfectly still assumes a second hand or stable surface — a discrete tap achieves the same outcome without either assumption.

questions.from: 3+ modules back — Content, Language and Reading
questions.prompt: A denial letter's rewrite is shorter and friendlier but no longer states the actual reason for the denial. What's the right read?

options.label: It's an improvement — shorter and friendlier is always more accessible
It's not genuine plain language — it deleted the information the reader needs to act, trading one failure for another
It's fine as long as it passes a readability score

questions.explanation: Plain language means stating necessary complexity clearly, not deleting it — a rewrite missing the actual reason has a different failure than the dense original, not a fix for it.

questions.from: 3+ modules back — Content, Language and Reading
questions.prompt: Ten 'Read more' links, each inside a paragraph naming a different headline, might pass WCAG 2.4.4. Why can this still be a real problem?

options.label: It isn't a problem once 2.4.4 passes
A link-list view strips away the surrounding paragraph entirely, so ten identical link texts defeat that navigation method even where in-context purpose is technically determinable
'Read more' always fails 2.4.4 regardless of context

questions.explanation: 2.4.9 exists specifically because link-list navigation removes all surrounding context — passing 2.4.4 doesn't mean link-list navigation still works.

questions.from: 3+ modules back — Content, Language and Reading
questions.prompt: Why is a word like 'adjudication' ordinary inside a claims department and genuine jargon in a denial letter to a first-time claimant?

options.label: Jargon is a fixed list of technical-sounding words, independent of audience
Jargon is relative to whether the actual reader is expected to already know the word — the same term can be ordinary in one context and genuine jargon in another
A word only counts as jargon once it fails a readability score

questions.explanation: The test is always whether the actual audience already knows the term, which is why the person who uses a word daily is worst-placed to notice it's jargon to someone else.

contentSections.body: None of these need to be perfect. What matters is which ones needed a guess — that's what the phase review will bring back.
